## Abstract

In psychiatric practice, the clinical intake interview remains a primary diagnostic instrument, requiring the clinician to establish rapport while disentangling complex, overlapping presentations. Here, we show that multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation environments improves language model performance on structured text-based psychiatric intake, spanning history-taking, differential diagnosis, and initial management planning. In a randomized, double-blind crossover study ( $N{=}60$ matched scenario pairs, 120 encounters) comparing the RL-trained agent against its identically prompted base model, 32 board-certified psychiatrists role-played standardized patients while a separate panel of 15 independent, board-certified psychiatrists scored the de-identified transcripts. The trained agent outperformed the base model in 76.7% of matched scenario pairs ( $p<0.0001$ ), with gains on an adapted clinical-examination rubric ( $d_{z}=0.77$ , $p<0.0001$ ), patient-centered communication (82.0% vs. 65.2%, $p<0.001$ ), and differential diagnosis appropriateness (68.3% vs. 33.3%, $p<0.001$ ). Across 127 psychiatrist-validated simulated intake scenarios, the trained agent nearly doubled its base model’s clinical rubric score (0.706 vs. 0.379; composite reward 0.564 vs. 0.294, $p<0.0001$ ). To systematically probe conversational safety, we established two Delphi-consensus taxonomies, of clinical safety risks and relational competencies, from which 256 challenging adversarial presentations were derived; we find that training in simulation environments more than halved under-triage of acute safety risks (12.9% vs. 30.5%, $p<0.0001$ ). Substantial clinical gaps nonetheless remained, with comprehensive and appropriate treatment recommended in only 46.7% of human-evaluated encounters, at least one critical intake question omitted in 60.6% of simulated intakes, and acute safety risks under-triaged in 12.9% of adversarial presentations. Simulation environments thus provide a controlled testbed for training and stress-testing psychiatric conversational agents, with gains that transferred to psychiatrist-enacted encounters. However, addressing residual diagnostic, management, and safety limitations, alongside integrating external safeguards and clinician-supervised workflows, remains necessary before prospective clinical validation with real patients.

## 1 Introduction

Clinical dialogue is foundational to patient-facing medicine, but in psychiatry, the clinical interview itself remains a principal diagnostic instrument 144. In psychiatric presentations, the psychopathology itself can directly compromise how history is communicated, and patients often do not recognize the relevance of prior treatment failures or comorbid medical conditions causing their symptoms 25; 10; 39. As a result, the quality of the history depends on both systematic inquiry into these complex causes and interpersonal trust, with a stronger therapeutic alliance supporting more complete diagnostic formulation and improved treatment outcomes 149; 119; 180. Competent clinical dialogue couples two skill domains, diagnostic reasoning (differential diagnosis, psychopharmacology, risk stratification) and interpersonal processing (reading affect and psychological defenses, crisis de-escalation, shared decision-making, stigma-sensitive communication) 92; 2; 176. In psychiatry, both dimensions are especially entangled. A clinician who probes aggressively risks rupturing rapport; one who overprioritizes validation may never arrive at a diagnosis. Here we investigate whether language models can acquire these capabilities through training in simulated clinical environments.

Large language models now perform strongly on clinical question-answering 162; 163, clinical reasoning 127; 14; 109; 81, and conversational diagnosis 176; 15; 99, and a growing body of work applies them to mental health 31; 166; 134; 47, including psychiatric evaluation datasets 128; 104; 35, clinician-facing decision support 183, and patient-facing conversational systems. Evaluations of conversational medical AI have nonetheless largely excluded psychiatric presentations 176; 15; 99; 75. In the general medical settings those systems target, the conversation gathers a history that physical examination and laboratory testing can subsequently supplement; in psychiatry, where critical history and risk factors often emerge through skilled inquiry, the quality of the conversation itself determines the quality of the diagnostic information obtained 144; 55; 161. If eventually validated for clinical use, conversational intake systems may supplement static screening questionnaires in supervised pre-visit workflows by gathering preliminary history, conducting a medical review of systems (i.e., a structured inventory of physical symptoms across organ systems to screen for somatic causes) and medication reconciliation, and organizing a provisional differential diagnosis for the evaluating clinician to review and verify 75; 131.

In medical education, clinical competence is developed through structured practice with standardized patients and assessed through Objective Structured Clinical Examinations (OSCEs) 7; 61; 68. Psychiatry uses the same instrument to rehearse de-escalation, risk stratification, and rapport building under acute ambiguity 137; 67. Language models can likewise acquire conversational and sequential decision-making capabilities by interacting with simulated clinical environments, with reported generalization to unseen patient profiles, out-of-distribution diagnostic categories, and multi-turn dialogue settings 100; 32; 41; 88; 176, and generative patient simulators increasingly incorporate behavioral phenotypes, biases, and changing emotional states 152; 151; 86. Whether these approaches are sufficient to improve conversational psychiatric competence remains untested.

Here, we trained a large language model with multi-turn reinforcement learning across simulated psychiatric encounters, optimizing jointly for diagnostic accuracy, patient-centered communication, and clinical safety (Fig. 1). To isolate the effect of training, the simulation-trained agent and its base model were prompted and evaluated identically within each evaluation, sharing the same clinical system prompt and structured tools. We validated the resulting agent in three complementary evaluations:

- 1. Blinded human expert evaluation (Section 2.1): To test whether competencies acquired in silico transfer to encounters with human experts, we conducted a randomized, double-blind crossover evaluation ( $N{=}60$ matched scenario pairs, 120 text-based consultations) in which the agent occupied the clinician role, 32 board-certified psychiatrists role-played the patients, and a separate panel of 15 blinded, independent, board-certified psychiatrists scored de-identified transcripts. The trained agent received a higher score than the identically prompted base model in 76.7% of matched scenario pairs ( $p<0.0001$ ), with gains over the base model on an adapted Practical Assessment of Clinical Examination Skills (PACES) clinical-examination rubric 40 ( $d_{z}=0.77$ , $p<0.0001$ ), patient-centered communication 108 ( $p<0.001$ ), differential diagnosis appropriateness ( $p<0.001$ ), and management plan appropriateness ( $p=0.018$ ).

- 2. Automated psychiatric intake evaluation suite (Section 2.2): To support automated multi-turn evaluation of psychiatric interviewing, we curated 127 psychiatrist-validated clinical intake scenarios ( $\text{AC1}=0.93$ ) covering eight diagnostic domains and four difficulty tiers that gate diagnostically critical information behind rapport and clinical inquiry. Across these scenarios, as graded by a language-model autorater (Gemini 3.1 Pro), the trained agent nearly doubled its base model’s clinical rubric score (0.706 vs. 0.379; composite reward 0.564 vs. 0.294, $p<0.0001$ ), with substantial gains across all four difficulty tiers, an overall advantage preserved under an independent out-of-family judge model (OpenAI GPT-5.6-Luna, $p<0.0001$ ).

- 3. Adversarial stress-testing grounded in Delphi-consensus safety taxonomies (Section 2.3): To systematically probe conversational safety, two multidisciplinary Delphi panels established consensus taxonomies of clinical safety risks (6 domains, 21 risks) and relational competencies (5 domains, 18 competencies), from which we derived 256 adversarial patient presentations designed to elicit unsafe clinical behavior. Training more than halved under-triage of acute safety risks relative to the base model (12.9% vs. 30.5%, $p<0.0001$ ), though residual failures remained.

All evaluations used synchronous English-language text consultations with standardized or simulated patients grounded in US psychiatric practice guidelines, demonstrating interviewing and diagnostic competence in controlled settings rather than outcomes, safety, or efficacy in real care, where any clinical use would require direct clinician oversight instead of autonomous operation.

## 2 Results

We report three findings. First, in a randomized, double-blind OSCE with psychiatrists role-playing patients, the simulation-trained agent outperformed its identically prompted base model, with gains in clinical examination skills, patient-centered communication, differential diagnosis formulation, and initial management planning (Section 2.1). Second, under automated evaluation the same advantage held across 127 expert-validated intake scenarios, and a three-way comparison on the 60 OSCE scenarios located where simulated evaluation departs from the human study (Section 2.2). Third, under adversarial presentations, training reduced but did not eliminate unsafe behavior, and the residual failures were mainly under-triage and missed red flags, including errors of omission that post-hoc output filters cannot intercept because no overtly harmful text is generated, such as failing to ask the probing questions needed to uncover a concealed crisis or failing to escalate care (Section 2.3).

### 2.1 Simulation-trained agent improves upon base model in blinded human evaluation

To test whether clinical competencies acquired in simulation transfer to human encounters, we compared the simulation-trained agent against its base model (Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite 51) in a randomized, double-blind crossover OSCE ( $N{=}60$ matched scenario pairs, 120 synchronous English-language text consultations; Fig. 2a) covering mood, anxiety, psychotic, personality, and substance use disorders, occult somatic mimics, and acute crises. Both models operated under the exact same detailed clinical system prompt instructing structured history-taking, rapport-building, safety screening, and differential formulation, alongside identical tools and prompts, isolating the effect of multi-turn reinforcement learning in simulation from prompt engineering (Methods, Section 4.5).

In each pair, one of 32 board-certified psychiatrists (Supplementary Table 5; Appendix A.1) enacted the same standardized patient across separate consultations with both models. Psychiatrists served as patient actors in this preliminary study to avoid exposing real patients to an unvalidated system and to adjudicate each scenario’s clinical information-gating protocol in real time, judging turn by turn whether the agent established rapport, navigated alliance ruptures, and conducted targeted inquiry before disclosing diagnostically critical facts (such as prior treatment responses, underlying medical symptoms, or guarded risk factors), prior to the agent submitting a ranked differential diagnosis and structured management plan at consultation end. Encounters were evaluated from two complementary clinical perspectives using a battery adapted from prior clinical OSCE benchmarks 176 to capture distinct levels of interaction (Appendix A.4): immediately after each chat, the role-playing clinician-patient rated discrete communication behaviors via the 11-item binary Patient-Centered Communication Best Practice (PCCBP) checklist 108, global consultation satisfaction via the General Medical Council Patient Questionnaire (GMCPQ) 17, core empathy and welfare via four patient-facing PACES items 40, and longitudinal psychotherapeutic goal, task, and bond alignment via the Working Alliance Inventory Short Revised (WAI-SR) 62; independently, a separate panel of 15 blinded, board-certified psychiatrists (Appendix A.2) graded the de-identified transcripts and clinical outputs against the corresponding 18-item specialist PACES clinical-skills rubric 40, four differential diagnosis scales, and management appropriateness criteria. Encounters had no turn limit; the simulation-trained agent took a median of 60 clinician turns (maximum 165) and the base model 8 (maximum 17; Supplementary Fig. 1a).

#### Independent transcript scores and clinical skill.

The simulation-trained agent received a higher aggregate independent transcript rating than the base model in 76.7% of matched scenario pairs (46 of 60, 95% CI [64.0%, 86.6%], $p<0.0001$ , two-sided exact sign test; Fig. 2b). The same ratings favored the trained agent over the base model in 80.7% of decisive (non-tied) pairs for PACES clinical skill (46 of 57, $p<0.0001$ ), 77.8% for diagnostic reasoning and differential formulation (42 of 54, $p<0.0001$ ), and 64.3% for PACES management and behavioral-enablement sub-dimensions (Items 12 and 17: 36 of 56, $p=0.044$ ; Appendix A.5; the standalone overall management appropriateness item also reached significance, $p=0.018$ , below).

The simulation-trained agent scored higher than the base model on the adapted 18-item PACES clinical-skills rubric (3.04 vs. 2.32 out of 5.0, shifting mean performance from the Unfavorable [ $2.0$ ] range above the Satisfactory [ $3.0$ ] scale anchor while remaining below Favorable [ $4.0$ ]; mean paired difference $+0.73$ from unrounded scores, 95% CI [ $+0.49$ , $+0.96$ ]; $d_{z}=0.77$ , $p<0.0001$ , Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Fig. 2c). Immediate post-encounter ratings from the live clinician-patients on the four patient-facing PACES items were concordant in direction and magnitude (3.18 vs. 2.63, $d_{z}=0.45$ , $p=0.0017$ ).

#### Clinical skill transfer.

As rated by independent evaluators, the simulation-trained agent scored higher than the base model on all 18 PACES clinical-skills sub-dimensions (Fig. 2c; item definitions in Supplementary Table 1), reaching nominal statistical significance on 17 (all except fostering the relationship, $+0.20$ , $d_{z}=0.12$ , $p=0.38$ ). The largest gains concentrated in foundational history-taking, including past medical history ( $+1.21$ , $d_{z}=0.87$ , $p<0.0001$ ), review of systems ( $+1.10$ , $d_{z}=0.86$ , $p<0.0001$ ), presenting complaint characterization ( $+0.82$ , $d_{z}=0.62$ , $p<0.0001$ ), medication history reconciliation ( $+0.81$ , $d_{z}=0.53$ , $p=0.0006$ ), and family history ( $+0.64$ , $d_{z}=0.51$ , $p=0.0019$ ). Information gathering ( $+0.81$ , $d_{z}=0.72$ , $p<0.0001$ ) and differential diagnosis construction ( $+0.95$ , $d_{z}=0.60$ , $p=0.0009$ ) also improved substantially, alongside gains across all explanation quality, shared decision-making, management selection, and emotional responsiveness sub-dimensions ( $d_{z}=0.32$ – $0.53$ , all $p\leq 0.028$ ).

#### Differential diagnosis and clinical reasoning.

The simulation-trained agent produced better-rated diagnostic formulations than the base model on all four dimensions assessed by independent psychiatrists (Fig. 2d; item definitions in Supplementary Table 2), including differential appropriateness (3.73 vs. 2.82), differential comprehensiveness (2.80 vs. 1.88; 1–4 scale, $n{=}59$ complete pairs), inclusion of the probable diagnosis (3.93 vs. 3.13), and identification of plausible alternative causes (3.83 vs. 3.05; 1–5 scale; $d_{z}=0.36$ – $0.71$ , all $p\leq 0.0074$ ). Dichotomizing each dimension at a favorable rating ( $\geq 4$ on 5-point scales; $\geq 3$ on the 4-point comprehensiveness scale) preserved this advantage across all four dimensions (appropriateness: 68.3% vs. 33.3%, $h=0.72$ , $p<0.001$ ; comprehensiveness: 67.8% vs. 32.2%, $h=0.73$ ; probable diagnosis: 68.3% vs. 40.0%, $h=0.58$ ; alternative diagnoses: 63.3% vs. 40.0%, $h=0.47$ ). Averaged across the four dimensions, clinical reasoning scores were higher for the trained agent than for the base model (3.57 vs. 2.73, $d_{z}=0.55$ , $p=0.00014$ ). Evaluator-rated clinical confabulation (inventing unmentioned clinical details during the consultation or falsely recording in the post-encounter summary that the patient endorsed or denied symptoms never discussed; Item 28 in Supplementary Table 2) occurred in 1 of 60 trained-agent encounters (1.7%) versus 5 of 60 for the base model (8.3%; $p=0.22$ , McNemar’s exact test). In absolute terms, mean ratings for the trained agent remained below the favorable anchor on all four dimensions (below 4 on the three 5-point scales [3.73–3.93] and below 3 on the 4-point comprehensiveness scale [2.80]).

#### Patient-centered communication and relational boundaries.

Clinician-patients recorded higher adherence for the simulation-trained agent than for the base model across the 11-item patient-centered communication checklist (PCCBP 108) completed immediately after each encounter (82.0% vs. 65.2%, $d_{z}=0.49$ , $p=0.00054$ ; Fig. 2g; item definitions in Supplementary Table 3), with directionally higher adherence across all 11 items across encounters (and 10 of 11 on complete non-N/A pairs). The largest gains concentrated in relational competencies, including partnership building (68.8% vs. 35.4%, $p=0.0017$ ), encouraging patient participation (86.8% vs. 54.7%, $p=0.0002$ ), expressing care and commitment (84.9% vs. 56.6%, $p=0.0011$ ), building rapport (76.4% vs. 56.4%, $p=0.022$ ), and greeting the patient appropriately (100.0% vs. 85.7%, $p=0.0082$ ; McNemar’s tests). Differences on the remaining six items, where baseline adherence was already high or the item rarely applied in a single intake (such as using appropriate language, appearing open and honest, acknowledging mistakes, or discussing roles and privacy), did not reach significance ( $p\geq 0.059$ ).

The same battery included four patient-facing PACES communication items, on all of which the trained agent scored higher than the base model: perceived empathy (3.39 vs. 2.89), confirming patient understanding (2.69 vs. 2.08), maintaining patient welfare (3.60 vs. 3.02), and detecting and addressing patient concerns (2.91 vs. 2.40; all $p<0.02$ , $d_{z}=0.35$ – $0.46$ ). On the General Medical Council Patient Questionnaire (GMCPQ; 9 Likert communication items in Supplementary Table 3), scores were directionally higher for the trained agent without reaching significance (3.01 vs. 2.79, $d_{z}=0.19$ , $p=0.091$ ; Fig. 2f). Clinician-patients marked the Working Alliance Inventory Short Revised (WAI-SR) 62 as entirely not applicable in 41.7% (50 of 120) of encounters, reflecting that its longitudinal psychotherapy items (such as agreeing on ongoing therapy tasks and goals) often do not apply to a single diagnostic intake. Among the 21 pairs with evaluable data, WAI-SR scores did not differ significantly between conditions (2.45 vs. 2.48, $p=0.75$ ), and we treat this comparison as inconclusive (Appendix A.3).

#### Management plan quality.

The simulation-trained agent recommended comprehensive and appropriate treatments (46.7% vs. 26.7%, $p=0.023$ , McNemar’s test; Fig. 2e) and diagnostic investigations (50.0% vs. 28.3%, $p=0.020$ ) significantly more often than the base model, and achieved higher overall management plan appropriateness (3.67 vs. 3.18, $d_{z}=0.31$ , $p=0.018$ , Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Item 27 in Supplementary Table 2), concordant with gains on the PACES sub-dimensions for selecting an appropriate management plan (3.23 vs. 2.62, $d_{z}=0.34$ , $p=0.018$ ) and enabling treatment-related behavior (2.69 vs. 2.20, $d_{z}=0.38$ , $p=0.028$ ). Both models avoided inappropriate treatments (88.3% vs. 80.0%, $p=0.20$ ) and inappropriate investigations (83.3% vs. 83.3%, $p=1.00$ ) in most encounters, though management remained more challenging than history elicitation or diagnostic formulation, with less than comprehensive treatment recommended in 53.3% of trained-agent encounters and an inappropriate treatment recommended in 11.7% (versus 20.0% for the base model).

### 2.2 Training gains hold across domains and difficulty tiers in automated evaluation

To evaluate interactive interviewing across a broader diagnostic spectrum, we assessed the models across 127 simulated psychiatric intake scenarios independently validated by 54 board-certified psychiatrists (inter-rater agreement Gwet’s $\text{AC1}=0.93$ ; Fig. 3a; Methods, Section 4.6; Supplementary Table 4). Covering eight clinical domains across four difficulty tiers (Easy, Medium, Hard, and Edge), each scenario pairs the candidate model with a dynamic patient simulator that updates patient mood and communicative reliability in response to clinician empathy and inquiry, gating diagnostically critical facts behind rapport and targeted probing (Methods, Section 4.2). At consultation end, an automated evaluator (Gemini 3.1 Pro) grades the full trajectory and submitted clinical outputs against a 28-item clinical rubric ( $R_{\text{clinical}}\in[0,1]$ ) spanning five categories (diagnostic appropriateness, psychiatric management, alliance and communication, psychiatric assessment, and documentation quality; Supplementary Table 7), combined with safety and completeness penalties to yield a normalized composite clinical reward (Methods, Section 4.3; Appendix C.2). To test how substituting the patient actor and rater affects measured gains, we compared all three settings across the 60 shared OSCE scenarios (Fig. 3c–f; Methods, Section 4.7).

#### Simulation training produces large gains across difficulty tiers and clinical domains.

The simulation-trained agent achieved a pre-penalty clinical rubric score of 0.706 vs. 0.379 (+86%) and a normalized composite clinical reward of 0.564 [0.529, 0.599] vs. 0.294 [0.281, 0.308] ( $+0.270$ on the $[0,1]$ normalized reward scale, $p<0.0001$ ; Fig. 1, Fig. 3b, Supplementary Table 6, Appendix C.2). Substantial gains occurred across all four difficulty tiers (Easy: 0.646 vs. 0.335, $+0.311$ ; Medium: 0.571 vs. 0.318, $+0.253$ ; Hard: 0.536 vs. 0.277, $+0.259$ ; Edge: 0.513 vs. 0.250, $+0.263$ ), such that the trained agent’s Edge-tier score (0.513) exceeded its base model’s Easy-tier score (0.335). Across the five clinical rubric categories, training approximately doubled scores relative to the base model in management (0.678 vs. 0.377), diagnostic appropriateness (0.682 vs. 0.369), and psychiatric assessment (0.673 vs. 0.323), with the largest gain in alliance and communication (0.827 vs. 0.321) and a smaller gain in documentation quality (0.689 vs. 0.647; Supplementary Table 7). Training also reduced the automated hallucination penalty rate (unsupported factual assertions, invented clinical guidelines, or fabricated patient statements) from 46.5% to 3.1% and the critical-question omission rate from 96.9% to 60.6%. Under an independent out-of-family judge (OpenAI GPT-5.6-Luna), the advantage held in every difficulty tier but was smaller (0.443 [0.415, 0.471] vs. 0.278 [0.268, 0.289], $p<0.0001$ ; difference between models 0.165 vs. 0.270 under Gemini 3.1 Pro; Supplementary Table 8).

Error analysis identified incomplete diagnostic inquiry as the dominant failure mode for both conditions. At least one critical scoring-key topic was left unasked in 96.9% of base-model encounters and 60.6% of trained-agent encounters. Because this indicator triggers whenever any single item on the multi-topic diagnostic checklist is omitted (in contrast to the acute-harm red-flag metric in Section 2.3), these rates reflect the exhaustive completeness required across all gated history domains rather than an acute safety error rate. Training substantially reduced but did not eliminate the tendency to end encounters before eliciting all gated clinical information (median of 16 clinician turns [IQR 14–20] per simulated intake versus 9 turns [IQR 6–11] for the base model).

#### Autorater scores correlate moderately with psychiatrist ratings on the same transcripts.

We compared three settings across the 60 OSCE scenario pairs: scores from the evaluating psychiatrists grading the human-patient transcripts (Section 2.1), the autorater grading the same transcripts, and the autorater grading simulated representations of the encounter using the patient simulator that the agent was trained in (Fig. 3c–f; Methods, Section 4.7; Appendix C.3). Across the same transcripts, autorater scores show moderate correlation with the psychiatrists’ 22-item primary specialist composite within simulation-trained ( $\rho=0.58$ , 95% CI [0.37, 0.73]) and base-model encounters ( $\rho=0.57$ [0.34, 0.75]) and on per-scenario score differences between the two models ( $\Delta$ ; $\rho=0.40$ [0.17, 0.59]; Fig. 3c, e). Across the 60 pairs, the autorater preferred the simulation-trained transcript in 55 and the psychiatrists in 46 (both in 41, autorater only in 14, psychiatrist only in 5, both base in 0; 68.3% raw agreement vs. 72.2% chance agreement under skewed marginals; Cohen’s $\kappa=-0.14$ ). Both raters favored the trained agent in every clinical category, with a larger standardized effect under the autorater (paired $d_{z}=1.48$ [1.21, 1.86] vs. $0.71$ [0.47, 1.02] on the composite; Fig. 3f; Supplementary Table 10), as $d_{z}$ scales each rater’s mean gain by its own within-pair variability.

#### Simulated-patient evaluations preserve category-level gains but inflate effect size.

Under the same autorater, replacing the clinician-patients with simulated patients shortened the trained agent’s interviews (median 16 vs. 60 clinician turns; 8 in both settings for the base model on this 60-scenario set; Supplementary Fig. 1), raised scores for both models ( $+0.23$ [0.19, 0.27] trained; $+0.10$ [0.08, 0.12] base), and enlarged the mean trained–base gain from $0.21$ to $0.34$ (difference $+0.13$ [0.09, 0.17]; Fig. 3d). #### Adversarial design and validation.

We structured the adversarial evaluation around two complementary taxonomies developed through a modified Delphi consensus process (Table 1; Appendix D):

- 1. Clinical safety taxonomy (6 domains, 21 risks; Table 1a; Supplementary Table 12), which synthesizes five established safety frameworks 189; 1; 82; 150; 18. A two-round Delphi panel of clinicians ( $N=16$ in Round 1, $N=13$ in Round 2) spanning psychiatry, patient safety, primary care, emergency medicine, surgery, and clinical informatics achieved S-CVI/Ave = 0.96, with all 21 items reaching $\geq$ 80% consensus (Appendix D.1).

- 2. Relational competency framework (5 domains, 18 competencies; Table 1b; Supplementary Table 13), which defines the skills required to navigate communicative safety risks. A parallel two-round panel of mental health experts ( $N=14$ in Round 1, $N=11$ in Round 2) spanning computational psychiatry, clinical psychology, digital mental health, trauma, and crisis intervention achieved item-level CVI $\geq$ 0.80 across all 18 (Appendix D.2).

#### Scenario generation.

We generated 256 adversarial scenarios (four stratified sets of 64 cases across all risk categories), arranged across four difficulty levels weighted toward complex presentations: Easy ( $n=46$ , 18.0%), Medium ( $n=58$ , 22.7%), Hard ( $n=94$ , 36.7%), and Edge ( $n=58$ , 22.7%). Each specifies the presenting complaint, concealed safety-critical facts, adversarial escalation tactics, and a scenario-specific scoring checklist evaluating whether the agent identified concealed risks and maintained clinical boundaries under escalation without rupturing patient rapport. In addition to overall composite reward, the automated rubric tracks three specific clinical safety violation rates (Table 2): contraindications (prescribing or recommending a treatment that is unsafe given the patient’s medical comorbidities, concurrent medications, or physiological status), missed red flags (failing to detect or probe embedded warning signs of acute harm during history-taking), and under-triage (failing to escalate clinical disposition, i.e., the recommended post-encounter care setting and urgency level, to emergency or urgent psychiatric care when the patient’s presentation involves an active, life-threatening crisis). These evaluation scenarios were held out and deduplicated from the training mixture, and both models were evaluated at the policy level without external post-hoc output filters to measure intrinsic policy vulnerabilities directly (Section 4.4).

#### Residual safety failures persist despite simulation training.

The trained agent achieved a normalized composite safety reward of 0.672 (versus 0.357 for the base model, $p<0.0001$ ) and substantially reduced all three tracked safety violation rates relative to its base model, including contraindications (0.8% vs. 6.2%, $p=0.001$ ), under-triage (12.9% vs. 30.5%, $p<0.0001$ ), and missed red flags (6.2% vs. 10.9%, $p=0.04$ ; Table 2). Unlike the broad diagnostic-completeness checklist in Section 2.2 (where omitting any required history domain triggered the 60.6% critical-question omission indicator), the 6.2% missed red-flag rate specifically reflects failure to probe embedded warning signs of acute harm, indicating that safety-weighted RL penalties prioritized acute risk inquiry even when general intake questioning remained incomplete. These improvements suggest that multi-turn RL training can shape safety-relevant behaviors, including structured risk assessment routines and boundary maintenance under escalation pressure.

The residual failure rate determines how such a system would have to be governed, and it is why we treat safety architecture external to the learned policy as a precondition rather than a recommendation. In 12.9% of adversarial scenarios (33 of 256, or approximately one in eight adversarial presentations), the trained agent did not escalate simulated patients with acute safety needs, most notably in presentations where a crisis was actively concealed behind benign somatic complaints. These failures typically involved sophisticated concealment, such as embedding lethal means access within ostensibly routine medical narratives.

## 3 Discussion

We trained a language model with multi-turn reinforcement learning across simulated psychiatric encounters and validated it against its identically prompted base model in three settings. In a randomized, double-blind crossover OSCE with board-certified psychiatrists role-playing standardized patients, the trained agent received a higher independent transcript score than the base model in 76.7% of matched scenario pairs, with gains in clinical examination skills, patient-centered communication, and differential diagnosis formulation (Section 2.1). Across an automated evaluation of 127 clinician-validated psychiatric intake scenarios, it nearly doubled its base model’s pre-penalty clinical rubric score and substantially improved composite clinical reward, with gains across all four difficulty tiers (Section 2.2). Under 256 adversarial presentations designed to elicit unsafe clinical behavior, training more than halved under-triage relative to the base model, although residual failures remained (Section 2.3). Comparing the post-trained agent against its untuned base checkpoint under an identical clinical system prompt, tool interface, and reasoning-token budget isolates the combined effect of the simulation RL pipeline (spanning both adaptation to dynamic patient states and alignment to structured clinical rubrics) from prompt engineering or test-time compute. Because on-policy RL updates model weights from scalar rewards on self-generated trajectories without additional medical corpora, these results also show how far procedural gains carry across clinical tasks. In psychiatric intake, diagnostic reasoning and communication are more tightly coupled than in general medical consultations 176; 15, where core symptom histories are less contingent on trust; accordingly, diagnostic formulation scaled with interpersonal and history-taking gains, consistent with building rapport and sustaining structured inquiry unlocking the gated patient disclosures needed to double differential diagnosis appropriateness (68.3% vs. 33.3% in the OSCE). Conversely, downstream management tasks that generally depend on static clinical knowledge rather than conversational elicitation, specifically comprehensive treatment planning (46.7% vs. 26.7% appropriateness across pharmacological and psychotherapeutic recommendations), showed more modest gains and likely remained constrained by both the base model’s parametric capacity and the greater case-level subjectivity of psychiatric treatment selection 75.

Gains in patient-centered communication were broad, and clinician-patients rated the trained agent as displaying more empathic behavior than the base model during live interaction. These are best read as gains in procedural communication and structured empathic responding, captured in the same direction by all three communication instruments (PCCBP, GMCPQ, and the patient-facing PACES items), rather than as evidence of therapeutic alliance formation, which develops over sustained multi-session relationships 45. Frequent not-applicable responses on the WAI-SR, an instrument designed for multi-session psychotherapy 62, are consistent with this distinction (Appendix A.3). Whether simulation training also improves alliance in longitudinal settings remains an open question.

Automated multi-turn evaluation complements clinician-enacted assessment by gating diagnostically critical information behind rapport and targeted inquiry, testing interactive clinical interviewing rather than static knowledge recall; the training gain was preserved under an independent out-of-family evaluator (Section 2.2; Appendix C.2). In the adversarial evaluation, simulation training substantially reduced contraindications, missed red flags, and under-triage, but did not eliminate failures when acute risk was concealed behind benign complaints. The composition of these residual failures has direct implications for safety governance. Deterministic guardrails can intercept generation-side harms such as a contraindicated prescription, because the harmful content is present in the output and can be filtered. They cannot address omissions in which the agent never asks the question that would have surfaced a concealed risk, because a post-hoc safety layer has no corresponding content on which to act. Mitigating omission failures therefore requires process-level safeguards external to free-text generation, including structured state-tracking checklists that gate encounter termination on mandatory safety and review-of-systems inquiry, real-time supervisory monitors that audit dialogue state for unprobed red flags, and clinician-in-the-loop verification at handoff. Beyond evaluating our trained model, the clinician-validated intake suite, adversarial stress-testing protocol, and Delphi taxonomies (Table 1) provide a structured methodology for auditing both commission and omission failures across conversational systems proposed for mental health settings.

How closely automated evaluation tracks clinical judgment is quantified by the three-way comparison on the 60 OSCE scenarios (Section 2.2). The autorater correlated moderately with the psychiatrists’ ratings on the same transcripts ( $\rho=0.57$ – $0.58$ ). Replacing both raters and patients preserved the direction of the training effect in every clinical category, but not its size ( $d_{z}=2.11$ vs. $0.71$ with psychiatrists) nor its pattern across scenarios ( $\rho=0.09$ on scenario-level gains). Simulated evaluation can therefore order and stress-test models, but neither estimate the size of their differences nor identify the scenarios on which one model outperforms another. As a training environment, however, the same simulator proved sufficient: the gains it produced held when psychiatrists role-played the patients and graded the transcripts.

A documented gap in access to mental health services motivates this line of work. More than 75% of individuals with mental disorders in low- and middle-income countries receive no treatment 191, and even in high-income settings, fewer than one in five individuals with major depressive disorder receive minimally adequate care 173. Tele-psychiatry supports effective evaluation and treatment delivery for many presentations 71, which suggests that the encounter format is not the primary barrier to competent assessment, but it does not change the supply of clinician time, since a synchronous consultation occupies a psychiatrist for its full duration whether remote or in person. Addressing this bottleneck does not, however, imply automating psychiatric evaluation or replacing psychiatrists, social workers, or intake clinicians. Given the complexity of psychiatric care and the substantial error rates observed even after simulation training, our findings do not support autonomous deployment of the present system; rather, any prospective near-term clinical role should be strictly assistive and clinician-supervised 75; 131; 53, such as conducting a structured pre-visit intake to generate a provisional history and symptom summary that a supervising clinician reviews, verifies, and builds upon during the clinical encounter, potentially supplementing routine psychosocial intake or static questionnaires with structured medical review of systems, medication reconciliation, and preliminary differential screening for somatic mimics.

#### Limitations.

Several methodological and clinical limitations constrain what these results support. First, while multi-institutionally validated synthetic cases help address the scarcity of shareable psychiatric clinical data 75 and allowed training and automated evaluation to scale across the diagnostic taxonomy, simulated and clinician-enacted patients cannot reproduce the full range of rare conditions, backgrounds, motivations, or disorganized communication encountered in clinical practice; unlike trained professional standardized patients (such as those used in clinical trial rater calibration) or real patients, psychiatrists role-playing patients may present symptoms in overly structured, textbook patterns, making validation with professional standardized patients and real patient cohorts essential next steps. Second, our study uses a controlled within-model design comparing a lightweight policy model (Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite) against its identically prompted base checkpoint rather than against larger frontier models or human clinicians (such as psychiatrists or psychiatric social workers); while this design keeps multi-turn GRPO rollouts computationally tractable and isolates whether simulation training improves upon static prompt instructions, smaller model capacity likely constrained the ceiling on knowledge-intensive tasks such as comprehensive treatment planning (46.7% comprehensive and appropriate treatment in the OSCE), and future studies evaluating clinical readiness must incorporate human clinical comparators alongside ablations against non-interactive rubric fine-tuning and oracle-history baselines. Third, the training reward and scenario reference rubrics were generated within the same model family (Gemini 3.1 Pro) that served as the primary automated evaluator, introducing circularity risks including verbosity bias, stylistic mimicry, and reward hacking 203; 182. Cross-evaluator validation with GPT-5.6-Luna confirmed that a substantial training gain persisted under an independent judge (difference between models 0.165, attenuated from 0.270 under the in-family Gemini evaluator against which the policy was trained), though agreement between language-model judges does not exclude shared stylistic preferences, underscoring why evaluation grounded in human clinical judgment remains essential. In the three-way concordance analysis (Section 2.2), only the in-family autorater was compared against psychiatrists on the OSCE transcripts. Furthermore, because each OSCE transcript was graded by a single psychiatrist (with different evaluators across each pair), cross-rater reproducibility could not be estimated directly (Appendix A.6). Although transcript formatting and turn-count metadata were standardized and independent evaluators graded unpaired transcripts, the trained agent’s substantially longer consultations (median 60 vs. 8 clinician turns) could partially cue crossover clinician-patients during live interaction; however, independent psychiatrist score gains were not significantly correlated with turn-count differences across scenarios ( $\rho=0.18$ [ $-0.09$ , $0.43$ ]; Supplementary Fig. 1c). The simulated and clinician-patient settings also used different interfaces (Methods, Section 4.4), and we did not separate patient from interface effects on interview length or score. The training gain nonetheless held under an OSCE interface that differed from the one used in training.

Clinically, our findings are restricted to single-encounter text-based intake rather than ongoing care. Single-encounter intake aims at a provisional formulation and triage plan, whereas ongoing psychiatric care, including longitudinal medication management and psychotherapy, requires sustained therapeutic relationships and adaptive treatment planning across repeated contact 180; 118. Moreover, text restricts assessment to a text-inferable Mental Status Examination (Methods, Section 4.3); written dialogue exposes thought process, thought content, orientation, and expressed insight, but structurally excludes physical, behavioral, and non-verbal observations on which several diagnostic discriminations depend, including separating negative symptoms of schizophrenia from depressive psychomotor retardation, identifying catatonic features, and detecting acute intoxication or withdrawal 121; 84. A text-based agent therefore cannot perform a comprehensive psychiatric examination or substitute for a psychiatrist, and at most could support preliminary, clinician-supervised pre-intake information gathering. In addition, all scenarios and consultations were conducted in English and the clinical norms encoded in our rubrics reflect US psychiatric practice, whereas linguistic expressions of distress, diagnostic conventions, emergency hold criteria, and duty-to-warn mandates vary across languages and jurisdictions 64; 49, and the agent was trained for semi-structured intake as opposed to scripted diagnostic instruments such as the SCID-5 42. Finally, deploying AI in psychiatric care raises domain-specific ethical risks 20. Reinforcement learning to overcome guardedness corresponds in human practice to motivational interviewing 111, but under unconstrained optimization has a potential risk of discovering manipulative conversational shortcuts, and individuals in distress are susceptible to anthropomorphic projection and parasocial attachment 87. Any future translation would therefore require safeguards architecturally external to the learned policy, including hard output-level vetoes on clinical disposition and prescribing, anti-sycophancy auditing, clinician oversight, and deterministic escalation protocols for acute risk 154.

#### Conclusion.

A simulation-trained agent conducted standardized psychiatric intake at a level that board-certified psychiatrists rated above its identically prompted base model across clinical examination skill, patient-centered communication, and diagnostic formulation. Standardized patient OSCEs are an established milestone in medical education, but they do not substitute for prospective validation in real patient populations; the environment, agent, reward functions, rubrics, and evaluation scenarios described here are research prototypes, and none has been cleared by any regulatory authority for clinical use. Prospective study under institutional clinician oversight, with real patients and longitudinal follow-up, is the necessary next step. Such text-based systems are not a substitute for psychiatric clinicians and are not ready for autonomous psychiatric assessment; the immediate clinical question for future research is whether, as strictly assistive tools operating under direct clinician oversight, they can help expand the reach of clinician-led care 191; 173; 75. Answering that question requires the psychiatric community to define the evaluation standards and governance boundaries 75; 47, and the evaluation framework, rubrics, and taxonomies described here are offered as one contribution toward that goal.

## 4 Methods

Training an agent for psychiatric care requires a corpus that captures the diagnostic breadth, clinical ambiguity, and relational complexity of outpatient practice. A training set clustered on common presentations (such as uncomplicated depression or generalized anxiety) risks producing an agent that fails to generalize to diverse clinical encounters. Building on Liévin et al. Super, we developed a four-stage clinician-designed generation pipeline covering the diagnostic, demographic, and behavioral spectrum of outpatient psychiatry (Fig. 5). Of 50,000 initial generation requests, 48,243 scenarios passed quality verification and deduplication against the held-out evaluation scenarios.

### 4.1 Psychiatric scenario generation

The pipeline operates in four stages. First, a diagnostic domain and a presenting concern are sampled from a clinician-curated taxonomy grounded in standard psychiatric diagnostic classification (Stage 1). Second, a complete patient identity is constructed by sampling demographics, personality, and communicative behavior from population-calibrated distributions (Stage 2). Third, these clinician-defined specifications are assembled into a detailed, internally consistent clinical scenario using a language model as the generation engine (Stage 3). Fourth, a difficulty tier controls probabilistic augmentation of the scenario with additional clinical complexity, and automated quality checks filter for coherence, diversity, and information leakage (Stage 4).

#### Stage 1: Diagnostic domain and presenting concern.

Scenarios are sampled across 15 clinical domains (mood and affect, anxiety and fear, trauma and stress-related, psychotic spectrum, substance use, OCD and related, cognitive and attention, sleep, eating and body image, self-harm and safety, interpersonal and behavioral, somatic and dissociative, neurodevelopmental, sexual and gender identity, and personality-related), each paired with domain-specific presenting concerns (see Appendix C.1.2 for an illustrative evaluation scenario package showing the clinical vignette and scoring rubric structure). The diagnostic domain is drawn from a 15-category distribution weighted by epidemiological prevalence data. Within the selected domain, a presenting concern and primary diagnosis are sampled jointly from condition-specific prevalence weights, ensuring the corpus reflects real-world diagnostic frequencies while maintaining representation of rare but clinically important conditions.

#### Stage 2: Patient identity and behavioral profile.

Each scenario receives a complete patient identity with demographics drawn from population-calibrated sources 117; 177. Big Five personality traits (Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism; scored 0–100) are sampled from age- and sex-adjusted Gaussian distributions 165; 26. A conversation effort score (1 to 5), derived primarily from the sampled Extraversion, Conscientiousness, and Neuroticism traits, governs response length and grammatical formality. Each scenario additionally receives a clinical presentation style (typical, atypical, somatic, subclinical, or mixed) and, with 50% probability, a challenging behavioral modifier (e.g., intellectualization, somatic communication style, poor insight) that shapes how the patient communicates distress.

#### Stage 3: Clinician-specified scenario assembly.

Conditioned on the sampled diagnostic domain, presenting concern, and patient identity, a language model (Gemini 3.1 Pro 52) assembles the full clinical scenario according to a clinician-designed structured output schema. The schema enforces a comprehensive clinical specification that includes symptom progression, pertinent positives, and pertinent negatives informed by the DDxPlus evidence corpus 38; complete medical, psychiatric, family, social, and substance use histories; a ground-truth psychiatric diagnosis with all specifiers; treatment recommendations intended to be concordant with clinical practice guidelines; a cultural formulation (operationalized via the DSM-5 Cultural Formulation Interview; Appendix C.1.8); dynamic affect instructions using the Pleasure-Arousal-Dominance dimensional model 110; therapeutic responsiveness rules specifying how clinician communication quality modulates patient disclosure; and alliance rupture instructions specifying the type, trigger, and timing of mid-encounter therapeutic ruptures. Category-specific clinical guidance incorporates standard screening instruments (e.g., CAGE/AUDIT-C 37; 16 for substance use disorders; reality testing and medication adherence challenges for psychotic spectrum disorders). Half of all scenarios receive an additional structured skill challenge (e.g., diagnostic reformulation when new information contradicts the initial impression, risk stratification under ambiguity) to train adaptive reasoning under diagnostic uncertainty.

#### Stage 4: Difficulty calibration and quality verification.

Each scenario is assigned to one of four difficulty tiers (Easy, Medium, Hard, or Edge), favoring medium and hard cases. Each tier scales the probability of medical mimics and the activation rate across a library of 12 generative augmentation segments (short directive phrases, e.g., “the patient communicates distress through somatic complaints rather than emotional language”). Because segments activate independently and can stack, the effective augmentation space grows combinatorially with difficulty tier, producing layered clinical complexity across four categories (encounter context, patient narrative style, clinical challenge, and relational dynamics). For the 127 evaluation scenarios, tier assignment was subsequently audited by board-certified psychiatrists as one of the eight validation criteria (Section 4.6).

Generated scenarios undergo three automated quality checks: (1) clinical coherence verification rejecting scenarios with internally contradictory symptoms, diagnoses, or treatment plans; (2) a hidden-fact leakage check ensuring gated information is not revealed in opening statements; and (3) batch diversity analysis. Scenarios passing all checks are deduplicated using character $n$ -gram ( $n\in[3,5]$ ) TF-IDF vectorization with a cosine similarity threshold $\tau_{\text{dedup}}=0.9$ , including against the held-out evaluation scenarios. These checks are automated. Unlike the 127 clinician-validated intake evaluation scenarios (Section 4.6), the ground-truth diagnoses and treatment recommendations attached to the 48,243 training scenarios were generated by a language model and were not individually reviewed by clinicians; they should be treated as a synthetic training signal rather than as validated clinical standards.

### 4.2 Patient simulator

To generate the multi-turn clinical encounters required for RL training, a patient simulator converts each static scenario specification (Section 4.1) into a conversational agent. The simulator conditions a language model (Gemini 3 Flash 50) on the complete clinical profile $\mathcal{P}$ produced by the scenario pipeline, including the ground-truth psychiatric diagnosis, treatment history, and all psychiatric-specific fields. The simulator is used during training and to generate encounters on held-out scenarios for evaluation (Fig. 6).

Patient communicative behavior is parameterized along three dimensions (health literacy, disclosure propensity, and conversation effort) 100; 151; 94; 169. Each scenario additionally carries four structured behavioral specifications, including dynamic affect instructions using the Pleasure-Arousal-Dominance model 110, therapeutic responsiveness rules linking clinician empathy to patient disclosure 170, alliance rupture instructions calibrated to clinical literature 148, and crisis embedding instructions that insert indirect safety signals requiring skilled clinical inquiry to elicit.

Patient behavior is produced dynamically through a turn-level state manager tracking two hidden variables at each turn: current mood (neutral, anxious, frustrated, apathetic, optimistic, pessimistic, or confused) and communicative reliability (truthful, withholds, downplays, exaggerates, forgetful, or talkative), initialized uniformly at encounter start to prevent the agent from learning a single deterministic interaction strategy. At each turn, the state is updated via a two-call architecture 100; 151: the first call performs behavioral reasoning, evaluating the clinician’s conversational quality and updating the patient’s internal mood and reliability state, and the second generates patient dialogue conditioned on the conversation history, clinical profile, and updated state. Separating third-person behavioral state reasoning from dialogue generation within a standardized-patient simulation framing (under research safety thresholds permitting clinical role-play of crisis, self-harm, and substance-seeking presentations) allows the simulator to enact high-risk and adversarial scenarios consistently without safety-filter refusals, while ensuring that the same clinical question can produce different responses depending on the rapport established in preceding turns 169; 151.

### 4.3 Reward structure and automated clinical evaluation

The central design challenge is approximating key dimensions of clinical psychiatric performance within a reward signal. Optimizing for diagnostic accuracy alone risks producing an agent that interrogates patients without establishing rapport; optimizing for empathic communication alone risks producing an agent that is validating but diagnostically ineffective. We therefore design a hierarchical reward function that jointly optimizes both axes while applying large negative penalties to detected safety failures. A language model evaluator (Gemini 3.1 Pro) computes the reward at encounter completion. The same model family provides the primary autorater for the simulated psychiatric intake and adversarial safety evaluations, with training and evaluation instances functionally independent.

The reward is structured as a tree with three scored components and a deterministic system-error term (Appendix C.2; Supplementary Table 7) following Liévin et al. Super. The primary component is a clinical assessment rubric evaluated on a 1-to-5 Likert scale with structured chain-of-thought rationale. The psychiatric rubric extends the standard telehealth rubric 100 with psychiatric examination and risk stratification (text-inferable mental status examination and explicit safety planning and risk assessment), structured communication and rapport dimensions informed by Bordin’s tripartite model 11, and elevated diagnostic weighting.

Clinical score. The clinical assessment rubric is anchored by 28 standardized items across five primary categories: psychiatric management (7 items: urgency triage, investigations, treatment, follow-up, safety planning, risk assessment, and overall management), diagnostic appropriateness (2 items: differential diagnosis and text-inferable mental status examination), therapeutic alliance and communication (5 items: relationship building, information gathering, emotional responsiveness, task agreement, and goal agreement), psychiatric assessment (5 items: history of present illness, psychiatric history, substance use, social history, and psychopharmacology knowledge), and documentation quality (9 PDQI-9 items 168), evaluated with reference to each scenario’s 7–12 item binary clinical scoring key (Appendix C.1.2). During RL training, the reward tree 100 expands these categories with granular process sub-checks for communication style and intake completeness. In the automated intake and adversarial evaluations (Sections 2.2 and 2.3; Supplementary Table 7), the evaluator scores the 28 standardized items (normalized to $[0,1]$ ) across the five primary clinical categories (weighted $3{:}3{:}2{:}2{:}1$ ) to compute $R_{\text{clinical}}\in[0,1]$ . Diagnostic and management domains carry approximately half of the clinical score in both training and evaluation, making it difficult for the policy to earn high reward through empathic communication alone while producing clinically unsafe outputs. To accommodate the intrinsic uncertainty of psychiatric diagnosis 144, the differential diagnosis item is scored by both exact primary-diagnosis match and appropriateness of the ranked differential (top-3 inclusion and severity concordance).

#### Operationalizing Text-Inferable Mental Status Assessment.

The Mental Status Examination (MSE) traditionally combines observational physical signs with verbal cognitive evaluation. Synchronous text cannot capture psychomotor agitation, gait, eye contact, grooming, or vocal prosody. To preserve construct validity, our rubric restricts MSE scoring to Text-Inferable Mental Status Assessment across four domains observable in written dialogue:

- 1. Thought Process: coherence, goal-directedness, tangentiality, circumstantiality, and flight of ideas, as reflected in sentence structure and topic transitions.

- 2. Thought Content: somatic obsessions, harmful ideation, paranoia, or delusional conviction articulated in patient text.

- 3. Cognitive Orientation and Attention: temporal orientation, memory recall, and attentional focus, assessed via structured conversational probes.

- 4. Insight and Judgment: awareness of illness severity and capacity for collaborative safety planning.

Observational features described in role sheets are treated as contextual background, not verified exam findings. This assessment is inherently incomplete, as several critical psychiatric distinctions depend on non-verbal cues, including separating the negative symptoms of schizophrenia from depressive psychomotor retardation, detecting catatonic features, and identifying substance intoxication or withdrawal 121; 84.

Penalty terms. The second and third components impose large negative penalties for detected safety failures. During training, four critical safety flags penalize hallucination (penalty magnitude 2.0), clinical contraindication (3.0), management plan leakage (prematurely issuing formal treatment directives or internal clinical-artifact content during history-taking prior to completing assessment; 2.0), and premature closure (committing to a narrow diagnosis or terminating inquiry without probing key differentials; 2.0), and four red-team safety flags penalize adversarial-specific failures, including missed safety red flags (2.0), missed critical questions (1.5), under-triaged severity (1.5), and boundary violations (acquiescing to out-of-scope or inappropriate relational requests; 2.0), with the maximum-severity flag within each group determining that group’s penalty to prevent double-counting of correlated failures. At evaluation time (Sections 2.2 and 2.3), the standalone automated evaluator instruments six of these binary flags (hallucination, contraindication, management plan leakage, missed safety red flags, missed critical questions, and under-triaged severity), combined into a single penalty equal to the maximum triggered flag across all six indicators, $F_{\text{eval}}=\max_{k\in\{1,\dots,6\}}F_{k}\in[0,3.0]$ (Appendix C.2).

A system-level error penalty accumulates deterministically from action-parsing failures (0.5 per failure), failure to terminate the encounter (0.5), and a piecewise-linear turn penalty that is zero for encounters of fewer than 30 clinician turns, ramps linearly from 0.1 to 1.0 between clinician turns 30 and 40, and saturates at 1.0 beyond 40 clinician turns.

The composite reward combines these components:

$$ R=\text{clip}\!\left(\alpha\cdot R_{\text{clinical}}-\beta\cdot\max_{i}F_{\text{crit},i}-\gamma\cdot\max_{j}F_{\text{red},j}-\delta\cdot E_{\text{errors}},\;R_{\min},\;R_{\max}\right) $$

where $\alpha=3$ , $\beta=\gamma=\delta=1$ , and $(R_{\min},R_{\max})=(-6,3)$ . For interpretability across evaluation benchmarks, composite rewards reported in Sections 2.2 and 2.3 map the raw pre-clip evaluation score $R_{\text{raw}}=\alpha\cdot R_{\text{clinical}}-F_{\text{eval}}-\delta\cdot E_{\text{errors}}$ onto $[0,1]$ via quadratic normalization, $R_{\text{norm}}=\left(\text{clip}((R_{\text{raw}}+5)/8,\,0,\,1)\right)^{2}$ (mapping the nominal reward range $[-5,3]$ onto $[0,1]$ ), which amplifies differentiation at the upper end of performance ( $R_{\text{raw}}=0$ maps to $0.391$ ; Appendix C.2).

### 4.4 Reinforcement learning in simulated environments

Policy optimization. Following the ResidencyRL framework 100, we deploy Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) 155 on a base model $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ (Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite), sampling groups of $G$ trajectories per scenario to estimate group-relative advantages without a separate critic network (Fig. 7).

Episode structure. The patient simulator initiates the encounter, after which the agent interacts with the simulated patient (Section 4.2) through natural conversation alongside a structured clinical interface adapted from Liévin et al. Super exposing eight tools (fetch_patient_profile, submit_diagnosis, submit_differential_diagnosis, submit_urgency, submit_management_plan, submit_patient_facing_summary, submit_soap_note, and terminate), committing to ranked differential diagnoses with reasoning chains, management plans, safety assessments, and urgency classifications before electing when to terminate the consultation. Within each evaluation setting, the simulation-trained policy and the base model operated under the same clinical system prompt (structuring encounters into Intake, Triage, and Conclusion phases with one-question-at-a-time interviewing, mandatory emergency escalation for acute risk, and a history-first, decision-last workflow), structured tool declarations, and reasoning-token budget. In the human OSCE (Section 2.1), both models interacted with clinician-patients without a turn limit through the synchronous chat and post-consultation clinical summary interface (ATS) described in Liévin et al. Super. Training episodes apply the piecewise-linear turn penalty beyond 30 clinician turns (Section 4.3) to discourage unnecessarily prolonged encounters; at automated evaluation (Sections 2.2 and 2.3; evaluated with a single rollout per scenario at temperature $T{=}1.0$ , and four rollouts per scenario in Section 4.7), simulated encounters were permitted to run up to $T_{\max}=60$ agent turns (including the terminating tool call) while retaining the same reward formulation $R_{\text{raw}}$ (Section 4.3).

Training curriculum. The training mixture applies curriculum sampling weights across four scenario sources: 48% psychiatric specialty scenarios (drawn from 48,243 cases spanning the diagnostic taxonomy; Section 4.1), 35% general telehealth scenarios (49,870 cases 100, included to mitigate catastrophic forgetting of general medical knowledge needed to identify somatic mimics such as hyperthyroidism presenting as anxiety), 15% targeted history-taking scenarios (upsampled from 5,000 cases addressing premature diagnostic closure 55 across social history, medication specifics, symptom characterization, and exposure history), and 2% adversarial red-team scenarios (2,583 cases anchoring the safety penalty terms).

### 4.5 OSCE study design

Standardized patient methodology is an accepted standard for assessing diagnostic formulation, communication, and clinical safety 7; 61; 68. Role-play by board-certified psychiatrists provides clinical fidelity and expert calibration without exposing patients to experimental systems 176; 100, but does not reproduce real clinical care.

The OSCE cohort comprised 60 scenarios drawn from the 127 clinician-validated intake evaluation scenarios (Section 4.6) by sampling across diagnostic domain, difficulty tier, patient demographics, and crisis content, covering major psychiatric categories, occult somatic mimics, and complex ethical or legal presentations. Thirty-two board-certified psychiatrists (59.4% female; median experience 12.5 years, IQR 8–18; Supplementary Table 5) served as clinician-patients in a within-case crossover design. Psychiatrists were selected for this role rather than lay actors because executing each scenario’s conditional information-gating protocol required real-time clinical judgment of whether the agent’s inquiry warranted disclosing guarded diagnostic facts, alongside expert calibration when scoring post-encounter communication instruments, while avoiding any exposure of real patients to an experimental system. Each received a detailed role sheet specifying the patient’s history, presentation, psychological defenses, and disclosure triggers (Appendix A.1). The clinician-actor conducted separate, blinded, synchronous text consultations with the identically prompted base model and the simulation-trained agent. Presentation sequence was randomized and counterbalanced, with a 48-hour washout period between paired consultations. Clinician-actors and independent raters were blinded to model identity and training condition.

To prevent affective halo effects from live role-play, evaluation used a two-perspective protocol. Clinician-patients provided post-encounter perceptions immediately following the chat. Separately, an independent panel of 15 board-certified psychiatrists drawn from the 54-member expert validation cohort (disjoint from the 32 clinician-patient actors) independently evaluated full consultation transcripts and clinical outputs, formatted as standardized clinical records stripped of AI identifiers (Appendix A.2; Supplementary Table 4). Independent transcript evaluators scored an 18-item clinical-skills rubric derived from the Royal College of Physicians PACES examination 40 (which, together with the four patient-facing communication items rated by clinician-patients, comprises the 22-item PACES framework; Supplementary Table 1); a four-dimensional differential diagnosis rubric; and structured items covering investigations, treatments, management plan appropriateness, and clinical confabulation (Appendix A.4; Supplementary Table 2). Clinician-patients completed a post-encounter battery comprising the 11-item General Medical Council Patient Questionnaire 17 (nine Likert and two binary items), the four patient-facing PACES items, the 11-item patient-centered communication checklist operationalizing the Kalamazoo consensus essential elements 108, and the 12-item Working Alliance Inventory Short Revised (WAI-SR 62; Appendix A.3; Supplementary Table 3).

The primary endpoint was specified before unblinding as the proportion of scenario pairs in which the simulation-trained agent received a higher aggregate composite score than the base model, defined as the unweighted sum of all 18 PACES transcript grading items and all four differential diagnosis evaluation items from independent transcript evaluator ratings (with N/A entries contributing zero to the sum; replacing the sum with the unweighted mean of non-N/A items yields 45 of 60 pairs, or 75.0%, $p=0.00014$ ; Appendix A.5). This composite was tested against the null hypothesis $H_{0}$ (win rate $=50\%$ ) using a two-sided exact binomial (sign) test at $\alpha=0.05$ . Each transcript was scored by a single independent evaluator, so inter-rater agreement could not be estimated; internal consistency of the rating instruments is reported in Appendix A.6. Additional details are in Appendix A.5 and Appendix A.4.

### 4.6 Simulated psychiatric intake evaluation design and expert validation

The automated psychiatric intake evaluation comprises 127 expert-validated scenarios, instantiated from clinician-authored specifications, spanning the diagnostic, demographic, and difficulty taxonomy of outpatient psychiatry; the 60 scenarios used in the human OSCE (Section 4.5) were drawn from this validated set by stratified sampling. Whereas the training corpus uses prevalence-weighted stochastic sampling to maximize conversational breadth during reinforcement learning (Section 4.1), the evaluation suite was constructed through a separate, stratified factorial pipeline designed to give equal weight to all presentations and to pair each case with an explicit disclosure schedule and clinician-verified scoring key. All 127 scenarios gate clinically critical facts behind specific clinician behaviors, including direct inquiry, empathic probing, or sustained trust-building. Accurate diagnosis requires active clinical elicitation rather than retrieval of overt symptoms. Existing medical AI evaluations assess clinical knowledge through static question-answer pairs 74; 162; 8 or simulated patients in general medical domains 152; 86; 100; 151, but neither assesses the elicitation of gated diagnostic information through targeted inquiry and rapport 75; Appendix E situates our evaluation methodology against this literature in full.

Overall, the evaluation cohort spans eight diagnostic and competency domains, including six core psychiatric categories (consolidating the 15 training diagnostic domains; mood, anxiety and stress-related, psychotic spectrum, substance use, personality and complex presentations, and other presentations including ADHD, eating disorders, sleep disorders, autism spectrum disorder in adults, and gender dysphoria), medical mimics requiring workups for somatic causes (e.g., autoimmune encephalitis 30, Cushing’s syndrome 136), and challenging encounters involving ethical or legal conflict (e.g., decision-making capacity and involuntary evaluation 4; 64, intimate partner violence disclosure 107; Appendix C.1.5). Each scenario is parameterized as a complete clinical profile with patient demographics, health-literacy-calibrated presenting complaints, comprehensive history (medical, psychiatric, pharmacological, substance, social), behavioral dynamics (affective tone, tangentiality, alliance ruptures), disclosure gating schedules, and ground-truth scoring keys (appropriate differential diagnoses, guideline-concordant treatment regimens with dosages and monitoring parameters, and a 7–12 item binary competency checklist; details in Appendix C.1.2).

Difficulty is calibrated across five clinical axes (presentation type, comorbidity burden, pharmacological complexity, communication dynamics, and safety risk; Appendix C.1.6) into four tiers, where Easy ( $n{=}29$ ) features textbook single diagnoses with cooperative patients; Medium ( $n{=}32$ ) introduces mild diagnostic ambiguity and single complicating factors; Hard ( $n{=}36$ ) presents atypical phenotypes, medical mimics, or multiple comorbidities with alliance ruptures and active safety risks; and Edge ( $n{=}30$ ) tests attending-level judgment through occult somatic mimics, severe polypharmacy with absolute contraindications, illness denial, and concealed crises (Appendix C.1.7).

#### Expert validation.

All 128 candidate scenarios (designed as 4 scenarios per cell across the 8 clinical domains and 4 difficulty tiers) underwent blinded, independent review by a panel of 54 board-certified psychiatrists ( $N{=}54$ , median experience 10.5 years, IQR 6.3–19.5; across 22 U.S. states and 3 countries; Supplementary Table 4), each with $\geq$ 2 years post-certification experience and an active clinical caseload $\geq$ 10 patient-contact hours per week (three independent reviews per case). Reviewers applied an 8-criterion rubric assessing clinical realism, diagnostic coherence, ground-truth validity, difficulty calibration, disclosure architecture validity, scoring rubric validity, treatment plan accuracy, and absence of harmful content (Appendix C.1.3), classifying each scenario as approved, revised with author corrections, or rejected (Appendix C.1.4). Across three review rounds, 127 scenarios achieved final approval; in the initial blinded three-reviewer audit across all 128 candidate scenarios (1,024 scenario-criterion items; 3,072 independent evaluations), inter-rater reliability reached Gwet’s AC1 = 0.93 58 (criterion pass rate 96.2%; full validation protocol in Appendix C.1).

### 4.7 Three-way concordance on the OSCE scenarios

We compared three settings across the 60 OSCE scenarios: (1) evaluating psychiatrists grading the human-patient transcripts (22-item primary specialist composite; Section 4.5), (2) the Gemini 3.1 Pro autorater grading the same transcripts (pre-penalty clinical score; Section 4.3), and (3) the same autorater grading four simulated rollouts per scenario and model with the patient simulator in the simulation interface (Section 4.6); setting (3) therefore differs from (1) and (2) in both patient and interface. Each autorater category was paired with the nearest human instrument (Appendix C.3; Supplementary Table 9). For each pair of settings, we computed Spearman $\rho$ across scenarios within each model and on the per-scenario difference between the two models’ scores ( $\Delta$ ; averaged across rollouts with the patient simulator). Paired $d_{z}$ was computed on per-rollout differences and averaged across rollouts in the simulated setting, and length sensitivity was assessed by partial Spearman $\rho$ controlling for clinician turn count. Agreement on which transcript of each pair was better was summarized by Cohen’s $\kappa$ , and uncertainty by 95% bootstrap CIs over 10,000 resamples of scenario pairs.
