## Appendix A Extended Methodology

### A.1 Psychiatrist-as-Patient Recruitment and Protocol

Board-certified psychiatrists were recruited to role-play patients in a blinded, counterbalanced, within-scenario crossover design. During the OSCE, clinician-patients received only the Patient Role Sheet specifying the patient’s clinical background, behavioral traits, disclosure rules (what to share freely versus what to reveal only if trust is established or if asked directly), communication style, and resistance patterns, without the ground-truth diagnostic or management scoring key. Although some clinician-patients had participated months earlier in scenario validation (where each reviewer inspected a small subset of candidate scenarios; Appendix C.1), each scenario’s two crossover encounters were enacted by the exact same clinician-patient under strict blinding to model identity and condition order, ensuring that any prior familiarity was held constant across paired conditions.

From the 127 expert-validated psychiatric intake evaluation scenarios (Appendix C.1), 60 were selected for the crossover OSCE via stratified sampling across diagnostic domain, difficulty tier, patient demographics, and crisis content. Each scenario produced two text-based encounters (one with the identically prompted base model and one with the RL-trained agent) in counterbalanced order with a mandatory 48-hour washout period. Post-encounter, clinician-patients completed the WAI-SR (Appendix A.3), GMCPQ (11 items; comprising nine 5-point Likert communication items used to compute the GMCPQ composite and two binary global retention items), PACES patient-facing communication and empathy items (4 items), and PCCBP patient-centered communication items (11 binary items). Clinician-patients also provided qualitative feedback.

### A.2 Evaluator Recruitment and Blinding

#### Eligibility and recruitment.

Board-certified psychiatrists were recruited through professional networks and clinical research platforms for three study roles: (1) OSCE transcript evaluation, (2) clinical intake scenario validation (Appendix C.1), and (3) OSCE standardized-patient role-play (Appendix A.1). Eligibility required: (a) current board certification in psychiatry (ABPN, AOBNP, MRCPsych, FRCPC, FRANZCP, or equivalent); (b) $\geq$ 2 years of post-certification practice; (c) active clinical caseload ( $\geq$ 10 patient-contact hours/week); and (d) no prior involvement in the AI system’s development. Recruitment targeted diversity across practice setting (academic, community, VA/government, inpatient, outpatient clinic, telehealth, private), patient population (adult general, addiction, child/adolescent, consultation-liaison, forensic, geriatric, neuropsychiatry), geographic region, and career stage. Evaluators who had published on AI in psychiatry within 24 months were excluded to minimize expectation bias. All evaluators provided informed consent and were compensated at standard consulting rates.

#### Expert pool demographics.

Full aggregate characteristics of the 54-member expert panel (which validated the clinical intake evaluation scenarios; Appendix C.1) are reported in Supplementary Table 4. A subset of $N=15$ board-certified psychiatrists from this pool (disjoint from the 32 clinician-patient actors) performed the OSCE transcript scoring described below. Because both roles drew on the same recruited panel, some transcript evaluators had previously participated in scenario validation, where reviewers inspected candidate vignettes and reference rubrics. However, standard OSCE transcript grading explicitly requires every evaluator to grade transcripts against the scenario’s validated clinical answer key (Appendix A.4). Evaluators were blinded to model identity and experimental condition in both roles, and the primary comparison is within-scenario, so any prior familiarity with scenario specifications applies to both conditions identically and cannot bias the between-condition contrast.

#### Blinding protocol.

Evaluators were blinded to: (a) the study hypothesis (they were informed only that the study compared “two conversational clinical AI systems for psychiatric encounters”); (b) experimental conditions (transcripts were identified only by random alphanumeric codes); (c) model identity (no information about training method, model architecture, or which system was expected to perform better was disclosed); and (d) pairing structure (evaluators were unaware that transcripts were paired by scenario). All transcripts underwent formatting standardization prior to human evaluation: system-generated formatting markers, turn-count indicators, and response-length metadata were removed. Line breaks, punctuation style, and header formatting were normalized to a common template. Transcripts were presented in independently randomized order for each evaluator, with no two evaluators receiving the same order. Although turn-count indicators and response-length metadata were stripped, overall transcript length (number of conversational exchanges) remained an intrinsic feature of each dialogue; its potential association with evaluator ratings was therefore explicitly tested in an encounter-length sensitivity analysis (Appendix C.3; Supplementary Fig. 1).

#### Calibration protocol.

Before scoring live transcripts, evaluators completed a two-stage calibration. In Stage 1, each evaluator independently scored 5 pilot transcripts spanning the quality range (1 poor, 2 moderate, 1 good, 1 ambiguous). In Stage 2, evaluators participated in a 90-minute calibration videoconference comparing pilot scores and focusing on: (a) anchoring each PACES, differential diagnosis, and management scale point to concrete clinical exemplars against the scenario answer key; (b) resolving rubric ambiguities from Stage 1; and (c) establishing consensus on boundary cases, including criteria for marking items “not applicable.” Pilot transcripts were excluded from analysis. The finalized rubric was distributed with exemplar anchors for each dimension.

#### Scoring procedure.

Each of the 120 transcripts (60 matched pairs $\times$ 2 conditions) was independently scored by a single board-certified psychiatrist evaluator from the 15-member grading cohort (disjoint from the clinician-patient pool). Evaluators were assigned transcripts in balanced blocks, independently of experimental condition, and no evaluator scored both members of a matched pair. Because each transcript was scored by one evaluator, classical inter-rater reliability metrics are not applicable; internal consistency reliability of the multi-item instruments is reported in Appendix A.6. Scoring was conducted through a secure web-based interface that enforced dimension-by-dimension scoring and recorded per-dimension completion times.

### A.3 Working Alliance Inventory (WAI-SR)

The Working Alliance Inventory – Short Revised (WAI-SR) 62 was administered to clinician-patients following each live encounter. WAI-SR data were available for 21 of 60 scenario pairs (35%); at the encounter level, 50 of 120 encounters (41.7%) returned all-not-applicable responses, and 70 produced at least one scored item. Clinician-patients marked psychotherapy-specific alliance items (e.g., collaborating on longitudinal therapy goals) as inapplicable to a single diagnostic intake encounter, consistent with their free-text feedback. Instrument position and respondent fatigue are unlikely explanations: the WAI-SR was administered as the first block, preceding the GMCPQ, PACES, and PCCBP ratings, all completed at high rates. Among evaluable pairs, the overall WAI-SR composite showed no significant difference between conditions (Simulation-trained: $2.45\pm 0.97$ ; Base model: $2.48\pm 1.31$ ; $p=0.75$ , Wilcoxon signed-rank test). This comparison is severely underpowered ( $n=21$ pairs), and the 65% pair-level non-response rate introduces potential non-response bias. The comparison is therefore inconclusive: attrition and sample size preclude confirming or ruling out a difference. Low WAI-SR scores for both conditions likely reflect inherent limitations of single-encounter text-based consultations for establishing therapeutic alliance, which typically develops over multiple sessions 45.

### A.4 Evaluation Instruments

Human OSCE encounters were evaluated using two standardized survey instruments adapted from the Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer (AMIE) randomized OSCE study 176: (1) an independent specialist psychiatrist transcript evaluation survey (Supplementary Tables 1 and 2) and (2) a clinician-patient post-encounter feedback survey completed immediately after each live consultation (Supplementary Table 3).

#### Independent specialist psychiatrist transcript evaluation survey.

Blinded psychiatrist evaluators graded each de-identified consultation transcript and submitted clinical summary against the scenario’s validated clinical answer key across 28 active items (Supplementary Tables 1 and 2):

- • PACES clinical consultation and communication skills (18 items; Supplementary Table 1): Adapted from the Royal College of Physicians Practical Assessment of Clinical Examination Skills (PACES) examination 40 and the AMIE specialist evaluation framework 176, evaluators answered “To what extent did the doctor…” across four subdomains: Clinical History Elicitation (5 items: presenting complaint, systems review, past medical history, family history, and medication history), Explanation of Relevant Clinical Information (5 items: explaining accurately, clearly, with structure, comprehensively, and professionally), Clinical Judgment (2 items: constructing a sensible differential diagnosis and selecting a comprehensive, sensible, and appropriate management plan), and Patient-Centered Communication Domains (6 items: fostering a relationship, gathering information, providing information, making decisions, enabling disease- and treatment-related behavior, and responding to emotions). All 18 items were rated on a 5-point scale (Very unfavorable [1], Unfavorable [2], Satisfactory [3], Favorable [4], Very favorable [5], or N/A). Together with the four patient-facing PACES items administered on the clinician-patient form, these items constitute the 22-item PACES framework.

- • Differential diagnosis quality and accuracy (4 items; Supplementary Table 2): Adapted directly from Tu et al. Super, evaluators rated: (1) differential diagnosis (DDx) appropriateness compared to the answer key (5-point scale from 1. Very Inappropriate to 5. ### A.5 Statistical Analysis

The primary outcome was the independent evaluator head-to-head win rate on overall clinical competence (proportion of scenario pairs in which the simulation-trained agent received a higher aggregate transcript rating than the base model across the 18 PACES and 4 differential diagnosis items; 46 of 60 pairs, 76.7%, 95% CI [64.0%, 86.6%], $p<0.0001$ ), tested against the null hypothesis of 50% using a two-sided exact binomial (sign) test. Replacing the unweighted item sum with the unweighted mean of non-N/A items yields a nearly identical head-to-head win rate (45 of 60 pairs, 75.0%, 95% CI [62.1%, 85.3%], $p=0.00014$ ). Secondary domain-level head-to-head win rates in Fig. 2b were evaluated with two-sided exact sign tests on decisive (non-tied) pairs for the 18-item PACES composite (46 of 57, 80.7%, $p<0.0001$ ), the 4-item differential diagnosis composite (42 of 54, 77.8%, $p<0.0001$ ), and the PACES management and behavioral-enablement sub-dimensions (Items 12 and 17 in Supplementary Table 1: selecting a comprehensive, sensible, and appropriate management plan and enabling disease- and treatment-related behavior; 36 of 56, 64.3%, $p=0.044$ ; concordant with the standalone 5-point overall management plan appropriateness item, Item 27 in Supplementary Table 2, which also reached significance: 3.67 vs. 3.18, $d_{z}=0.31$ , $p=0.018$ ). Secondary continuous outcomes included domain-specific Likert scores (computed per encounter as the mean across non-N/A items) analyzed with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on matched pairs. Individual binary communication items (PCCBP; complete non-N/A pairs), binary safety-avoidance items (Items 24 and 26), and dichotomized 3-point investigations and treatments items (Items 23 and 25 in Supplementary Table 2, dichotomized at the top category: 3 = Yes, comprehensive and appropriate vs. 1–2 = No, did not recommend or recommended but not comprehensive) were compared between paired encounters using McNemar’s $\chi^{2}$ test without continuity correction; the sparse clinical confabulation flag (Item 28) was compared using McNemar’s exact binomial test. Effect sizes are reported with the estimator matched to the outcome scale. For continuous outcomes measured on matched pairs we report the paired standardized mean difference

$$ d_{z}=\frac{\mu_{\Delta}}{\sigma_{\Delta}},\qquad\Delta_{i}=x_{i}^{\text{RL}}-x_{i}^{\text{base}}, $$

where $\mu_{\Delta}$ and $\sigma_{\Delta}$ are the mean and standard deviation of the $N=60$ within-pair differences. Because $d_{z}$ standardizes by the variability of the paired differences rather than by the between-encounter variability, it is not interchangeable with the independent-samples Cohen’s $d$ computed on the same data; for the PACES composite the two estimators give $d_{z}=0.77$ and $d=0.97$ (where $d_{z}<d$ because different evaluators graded the two transcripts in each pair, so inter-rater variance enters $\sigma_{\Delta}$ ). We report $d_{z}$ throughout because the crossover design matches encounters within scenario. For binary or dichotomized proportions we report the arcsine-transformed difference

$$ h=2\arcsin\sqrt{p_{1}}-2\arcsin\sqrt{p_{2}}, $$

which is variance-stabilizing and therefore comparable across base rates. All effect sizes are accompanied by 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (10,000 resamples). In the automated simulated intake ( $N{=}127$ ; Section 2.2) and adversarial safety ( $N{=}256$ ; Section 2.3) evaluations, the simulation-trained agent and base model were likewise compared across matched scenarios using two-sided paired tests with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over 10,000 scenario resamples. Secondary and exploratory endpoints were not corrected for multiple comparisons: the study was powered for a single pre-specified primary endpoint, and all secondary $p$ -values are reported as nominal and interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.

### A.6 Instrument Reliability for OSCE Transcript Ratings

Each OSCE transcript was scored by a single independent psychiatrist evaluator using the structured rating instruments described in Methods, Section 4.5. Because the study design assigned one evaluator per transcript (rather than multiple evaluators per transcript), classical inter-rater reliability metrics (e.g., ICC between raters) are not applicable. Instead, we assessed internal consistency reliability of the multi-item rating instruments.

The 18-item PACES-derived clinical skills rubric showed high internal consistency (Cronbach’s $\alpha=0.963$ , $k=18$ items, $N=70$ complete cases), consistent with individual PACES sub-dimensions loading on a coherent construct. The complete-case $N$ is lower than 120 because evaluators could mark items “not applicable” when a transcript provided no scoring basis; per-item $N$ ranged from 102 to 119. Composite and per-dimension analyses used all available ratings rather than restricting to complete cases. The four-item differential diagnosis rubric also showed high consistency ( $\alpha=0.925$ , $k=4$ , $N=119$ ). Two caveats apply. First, because each transcript was scored by one evaluator, we cannot estimate cross-rater reproducibility, and residual rater variance is unquantified. Second, $\alpha$ values above 0.95 conventionally suggest item redundancy or halo effects rather than instrument quality, so these coefficients should not be read as validating the rubric’s discriminant validity. Both limitations apply equally to both conditions and are unlikely to bias the within-scenario contrast, but they limit the precision of absolute score interpretation.

## Appendix C Simulated Psychiatric Intake Evaluation Suite

### C.1 Case Generation Protocol for Intake Evaluation

This appendix describes the methodology for generating and validating the 127 expert-curated scenarios that constitute the simulated psychiatric intake evaluation suite. These evaluation scenarios are distinct from the 48,243 training scenarios generated through the automated four-stage pipeline (Methods, Section 4.1); the evaluation cohort requires clinical-grade rigor and human expert validation at every stage.

#### C.1.1 Overview

The scenario construction process produced an initial pool of 128 candidate scenario specifications (32 per difficulty tier) using a structured specification-then-instantiation process. Specifications were designed by clinicians to cover the diagnostic, demographic, and difficulty taxonomy of outpatient psychiatry. A language model (Gemini 3.1 Pro 52) instantiated these specifications into complete scenario packages, each comprising a clinical vignette (the patient role sheet presented to the patient simulator or role-playing clinician-patient) and a scoring rubric (the ground-truth reference used for evaluation). Expert review across three iterative rounds (round 1: 89 approved, 38 revised, 1 rejected; round 2: 27 approved, 11 revised; round 3: 11 approved) validated, revised, or filtered candidates to yield the final 127-scenario evaluation set (99.2% net retention rate; 1 scenario rejected).

#### C.1.2 Scenario package structure

Each candidate scenario consisted of two documents delivered together to expert reviewers.

Clinical vignette (patient role sheet). The vignette presents the patient’s full profile in structured plain text:

- • Identity header: name, age, sex, ethnicity, occupation, living situation, and chief complaint phrased in lay language.

- • Opening statement: the patient’s self-presentation at encounter initiation, written in first person, reflecting their lay framing of distress and interpersonal posture toward clinicians.

- • Social and contextual background: housing, employment, daily routine, substance use, exercise, and diet relevant to the clinical picture.

- • Medical and psychiatric history: current and past diagnoses, prior psychiatric episodes, surgical history.

- • Current medications: full medication list with doses, including any medications that create pharmacological complexity (e.g., drug-drug interaction traps, contraindication scenarios).

- • Allergies, family history, and expectations: the patient’s stated fears, anticipated outcome, and interpersonal stance toward the evaluation.

- • Scripted patient questions: 2–4 in-character questions the patient will raise during the encounter, designed to test boundary maintenance or diagnostic probing.

- • Disclosure architecture: explicit rules specifying which clinical information is available freely, which requires the clinician to ask a specific targeted question, and which is only revealed after the clinician establishes rapport by validating the patient’s concerns. Each piece of trust-gated information includes the precise condition under which it unlocks (e.g., “reveal the prednisone timeline only if the clinician validates frustration with the evaluation and explains the medical rationale for the question”).

- • Observable behavioral cues: text-based behavioral markers the patient exhibits (e.g., rapid message cadence, capitalization, circumlocution, terse deflection) that a clinician should interpret as psychiatric signs.

Scoring rubric. The rubric provides the ground-truth reference against which agent performance is evaluated:

- • Primary diagnosis: ICD-10-CM code and full specifiers.

- • Active comorbid conditions: concurrent medical or psychiatric diagnoses relevant to management.

- • Ranked differential diagnosis: at least three plausible alternatives with brief rationale for each.

- • Evidence-based treatment plan: specific first-line and alternative pharmacological or psychotherapeutic interventions, dosing guidance, contraindicated agents with explicit rationale (e.g., absolute contraindications due to drug-drug interactions).

- • Clinical risk assessment: current suicidality, homicidality, and psychosocial risk factors.

- • Recommended investigations: in-visit text-based screening tools (e.g., C-SSRS, PHQ-9 administered via text) and laboratory or imaging studies to order.

- • Follow-up plan: timing and modality of next encounter.

- • Binary scoring checklist: 7–12 items (typically 8–12) specifying the concrete clinical actions a competent clinician must complete during the encounter. Each item is directly observable from the encounter transcript (e.g., “Elicits the timeline of the patient’s asthma exacerbation and recent initiation of high-dose prednisone to identify the substance-induced etiology of the mania.”). Items are written to resist credit for superficially correct but clinically inadequate responses: the criterion specifies the target clinical information, not merely the topic area.

An illustrative complete scenario package, including clinical vignette and full scoring rubric, is provided in the following example. The scenario depicts a 27-year-old male software developer presenting for mandatory psychiatric clearance, with a concealed steroid-induced manic episode and a high-risk drug interaction trap (Lithium carries a clinically significant risk with concurrent HCTZ and Losartan).

#### Expert reviewer qualifications.

Each candidate scenario was reviewed by three independent, board-certified psychiatrists (ABPN or international equivalent; $\geq$ 2 years post-certification; active clinical caseload $\geq$ 10 patient-contact hours/week; no involvement in AI system development). Reviewers operated independently with no access to other reviewers’ assessments. Expert panel demographics are reported in Appendix B; inter-rater reliability for scenario validation (Gwet’s AC1) is reported in Methods, Section 4.6.

#### C.1.3 Validation rubric

Each reviewer scored every scenario on 8 criteria using defined scales with minimum thresholds. All 8 criteria must meet threshold for a scenario to receive an APPROVE verdict.

#### Criterion 1: Clinical Realism

“Could a patient matching this description present to a psychiatric clinic with these symptoms, history, and circumstances?”

| Score | Definition |
|---|---|
| 1 | The combination of symptoms, demographics, and history is clinically implausible (e.g., a 19-year-old with 15 years of treatment-resistant schizophrenia). |
| 2 | The presentation is theoretically possible but would be extremely rare and would raise immediate suspicion in a clinical setting. |
| 3 | The presentation is clinically plausible but contains minor elements that feel artificial or contrived. |
| 4 | The presentation reads like a real patient; nothing jumps out as implausible. |
| 5 | The presentation is so clinically detailed and realistic it could serve as a teaching case. |

Threshold: $\geq$ 4. Common failures: age-impossible diagnoses (e.g., personality disorder diagnosed at age 12); medication regimens no competent physician would prescribe (e.g., two concurrent SSRIs without rationale); symptom timelines violating standard DSM-5-TR duration criteria (e.g., two days of elevated mood diagnosed as Bipolar I mania in the absence of hospitalization or psychotic features, or two weeks of generalized worry diagnosed as GAD); internally inconsistent demographic details (e.g., “retired” + age 28).

#### Criterion 2: Diagnostic Coherence

“Are the listed symptoms, pertinent positives, pertinent negatives, and history internally consistent with the ground-truth diagnosis?”

| Score | Definition |
|---|---|
| 1 | Symptoms directly contradict the listed diagnosis. |
| 2 | Symptoms are vaguely consistent but important diagnostic criteria are missing. |
| 3 | Most standard diagnostic criteria are met, but there are minor gaps or inconsistencies. |
| 4 | All relevant diagnostic criteria are clearly represented in the symptom profile. |
| 5 | Symptoms map precisely to standard diagnostic criteria; pertinent negatives actively rule out key differentials. |

Threshold: $\geq$ 3. Reviewers check: (a) symptom timeline meets diagnostic duration requirements (e.g., MDD $\geq$ 2 weeks); (b) sufficient diagnostic criteria are present (e.g., MDD requires $\geq$ 5 of 9 criteria); (c) pertinent negatives are consistent with the primary diagnosis rather than an alternative; and (d) the differential list includes reasonable alternatives.

#### Criterion 3: Ground-Truth Validity

“Is the listed diagnosis the most likely primary diagnosis given the full clinical picture?”

Responses: Agree / Partially agree / Disagree. Threshold: Agree or Partially agree. Partially agree and Disagree responses require a documented preferred diagnosis with ICD-10-CM code and 2–3 sentence rationale. This is treated as one of the most valuable outputs of the review process: reviewer disagreements surface genuinely ambiguous presentations and trigger re-evaluation of the ground-truth assignment.

#### Criterion 4: Difficulty Calibration

“Does the assigned difficulty tier accurately reflect the clinical complexity?”

Responses: Correct / Off by 1. Threshold: Correct. Off-by-1 responses specify the direction of miscalibration. Tier definitions follow Appendix C.1.7. A PGY-2 resident should manage Easy cases competently; Edge cases would challenge experienced attending psychiatrists.

#### Criterion 5: Disclosure Architecture Validity

“Is the stratification of information (free / inquiry-gated / trust-gated) clinically realistic, and does it produce meaningful differences in encounter difficulty?”

Scale: 1–5 Likert. Threshold: $\geq$ 4. A score of 4 requires that trust-gated information is withheld in a manner consistent with real patient behavior and that its elicitation requires specific clinical skill. A score of 3 or below indicates that the gating conditions are arbitrary or that the information would plausibly be volunteered by any real patient without targeted inquiry.

#### Criterion 6: Scoring Rubric Validity

“Are the checklist items observable from the transcript, correctly linked to clinical actions, and resistant to credit from clinically inadequate responses?”

Scale: 1–5 Likert. Threshold: $\geq$ 4. Rubric items must specify the target clinical information, not merely the topic area. An item reading “asks about sleep” earns a score of 2; an item reading “confirms decreased need for sleep (patient reports 1–2 hours per night, feels fully rested)” earns a score of 4–5.

#### Criterion 7: Treatment Plan Accuracy

“Does the treatment plan reflect current clinical practice guidelines?”

Scale: 1–5 Likert. Threshold: $\geq$ 4. Reviewers check medication choices, dosing, contraindication documentation, and concordance with APA, NICE, or CANMAT guidelines as applicable. Drug interaction traps embedded in the scenario (as clinical challenge elements) must be correctly identified as contraindications in the rubric.

#### Criterion 8: Absence of Harmful Content

“Does the scenario avoid modeling clinical errors as ground truth, providing harmful advice, or containing content harmful if viewed out of context?”

Response: Pass / Fail. Threshold: Pass. Automatic rejection if a scenario presents a dangerous clinical error (e.g., prescribing an absolutely contraindicated medication) as the correct management without explicit labeling as an educational trap.

#### C.1.4 Review outcomes and acceptance rule

For each scenario, each of the three independent reviewers assigned one of three outcomes:

- • APPROVE: Passes all 8 criteria. The scenario enters the final evaluation set without modification.

- • REVISE: Fails 1–3 criteria, salvageable. The reviewer provides specific revision instructions. The revised scenario is returned for re-review by the same reviewer.

- • REJECT: Fails $\geq$ 4 criteria or contains a fundamental clinical error. The scenario is discarded from the evaluation suite.

Final acceptance rule. At least 2 of 3 reviewers must assign APPROVE (directly or after revision accepted) for a scenario to enter the final evaluation suite. Scenarios with majority REJECT verdicts are discarded. The expert panel conducted 128 candidate scenario evaluations across three review rounds (round 1: 89 approved, 38 revised, 1 rejected; round 2: 27 approved, 11 revised; round 3: 11 approved) to produce the final 127-scenario evaluation suite (99.2% net retention rate; 1 scenario rejected). Expert panel demographics are reported in Appendix B.

#### C.1.5 Diagnostic and Competency Categories

The simulated psychiatric intake evaluation spans 8 categories covering the breadth of outpatient psychiatric practice. Six categories target core diagnostic domains:

- 1. Mood Disorders: Major depressive disorder across episode types (single, recurrent, with anxious distress, with melancholic features, with psychotic features, with peripartum onset), bipolar spectrum including bipolar I, bipolar II, cyclothymic disorder, and premenstrual dysphoric disorder.

- 2. Anxiety and Stress-Related Disorders: Generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, illness anxiety disorder, and adjustment disorders across subtypes.

- 3. Psychotic Spectrum: Schizophrenia across presentation subtypes (paranoid, disorganized, catatonic features, negative-symptom-predominant), schizoaffective disorder, delusional disorder, brief psychotic disorder, and substance-induced psychosis.

- 4. Substance Use Disorders: Alcohol, opioid, stimulant, cannabis, benzodiazepine, and polysubstance use disorders, including substance-induced mood presentations and dual-diagnosis scenarios.

- 5. Personality and Complex Presentations: Borderline, antisocial, narcissistic, avoidant, dependent, and obsessive-compulsive personality disorders; complex PTSD; dissociative presentations; and somatic symptom disorder.

- 6. Other Presentations: ADHD across subtypes (predominantly inattentive, combined, late-diagnosis adult), eating disorders (anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge eating disorder), sleep disorders, autism spectrum disorder in adults, and gender dysphoria.

Two additional categories test competencies that transcend diagnostic boundaries:

- 7. Medical Mimics: Somatic conditions presenting as psychiatric illness, including endocrine mimics (hypothyroidism presenting as depression, Cushing’s syndrome presenting as psychosis), autoimmune mimics (autoimmune encephalitis mimicking acute psychosis, lupus cerebritis presenting as mood disorder), neurological mimics (frontotemporal dementia presenting as personality change, Wilson’s disease presenting as psychiatric illness), and iatrogenic mimics (steroid-induced mania, SSRI discontinuation syndrome mimicking relapse, medication-induced akathisia mimicking anxiety). This category specifically tests whether clinicians pursue the medical workup necessary to identify non-psychiatric etiologies, a critical competency that purely psychiatric evaluations do not assess.

- 8. Challenging Encounters: High-stakes clinical situations including acute safety crisis (active risk with plan and means), intimate partner violence (IPV) disclosure during unrelated visit, involuntary psychiatric evaluation, treatment refusal with active psychosis, malingering with secondary gain motive, and caregiver burnout with compassion fatigue. This category tests clinical judgment under conditions of interpersonal conflict, legal complexity, and competing ethical obligations.

#### C.1.6 Clinical Specification Framework

Each scenario was constructed according to a five-axis clinical specification framework:

- • Axis 1 (Presentation Type): Specifies diagnostic complexity, ranging from standard textbook presentations to obscure somatic mimics or highly atypical cases where standard diagnostic cues are absent or distorted.

- • Axis 2 (Comorbidity Burden): Controls the number and severity of co-occurring conditions, from none (Easy) to 2–3 interacting conditions that compound safety risk and restrict available treatment paths (Edge).

- • Axis 3 (Pharmacological Complexity): Ranges from straightforward first-line prescribing to extreme prescribing traps involving severe drug-drug interactions embedded in the patient’s medication list (e.g., a patient on hydrochlorothiazide and losartan for whom lithium carries a clinically significant risk of toxic accumulation and is therefore not the preferred agent).

- • Axis 4 (Communication Dynamics): Specifies the patient’s cooperativeness (scored 1–5 on an effort scale), alliance rupture type and severity, and behavioral presentation through text.

- • Axis 5 (Crisis and Safety Risk): Ranges from no safety concern to high-severity crises in which the patient actively minimizes or conceals acute risk, requiring sensitive elicitation.

#### C.1.7 Difficulty Tier Specifications

Scenario complexity is varied across four tiers defined along the five clinical axes above. The initial pool of 128 specifications (32 per tier) was submitted for expert review; one was rejected, and reviewer feedback prompted reclassification of several scenarios across tiers, yielding the final distribution below.

#### Easy ( $n=29$ ).

Textbook-concordant cases with a single diagnosis, no comorbidities, standard first-line pharmacotherapy, cooperative patients, and no acute safety concerns. A PGY-2 psychiatry resident should manage these competently.

#### Medium ( $n=32$ ).

Mild diagnostic ambiguity, a single complicating factor (one comorbidity, one prior treatment failure, or mild patient defensiveness), and occasional passive safety concerns.

#### Hard ( $n=36$ ).

Significant diagnostic complexity (atypical presentations, medical mimics, or multiple comorbidities), pharmacological constraints (treatment resistance, drug-drug interactions, or relative contraindications), and moderate alliance ruptures (hostility upon inquiry, clinician competence challenges, or controlled substance demands). Active safety concerns (crisis presentations with vague plan, NSSI disclosure, intimate partner violence) are present in approximately 75% of hard scenarios.

#### Edge ( $n=30$ ).

The most clinically demanding tier: obscure somatic mimics or metabolic traps, severe polypharmacy with absolute prescribing contraindications, severe alliance ruptures (total denial of illness, deep system mistrust, paranoid medication resistance), and high-severity hidden safety crises requiring emergency intervention. These are cases that would challenge even experienced attending psychiatrists.

#### C.1.8 Cultural Formulation and Equity Architecture

Rather than treating culture as superficial demographic metadata, the scenario generation engine embeds cultural factors into patient role sheets, clinical reasoning paths, and disclosure architectures across four domains:

- 1. Cultural Identity of the Individual: Incorporates racial, ethnic, linguistic, and migration background, including acculturation stressors, generational discordance, and intersectional social positions.

- 2. Cultural Conceptualizations of Distress: Integrates culturally shaped idioms of distress and lay explanatory models. For example, somatic presentations such as susto (fright sickness) in Latin American cultural contexts, shenjing shuairuo (weakness of the nervous system) in East Asian contexts, or idioms such as “thinking too much” or “heart dropping” are modeled as legitimate lay clinical expressions rather than misclassified as primary delusional content.

- 3. Psychosocial Stressors and Vulnerability/Resilience: Identifies cultural features that modulate help-seeking, including community stigma regarding mental healthcare, spiritual or faith-based coping mechanisms, family or elder authority structures, and systemic healthcare mistrust.

- 4. Cultural Features of the Clinical Relationship: Calibrates the patient’s interpersonal posture toward the clinician, including power differentials, deference to perceived medical authority, or expectations regarding conversational pacing and formality.

#### Generation prompt specification.

The scenario generator operationalizes these domains via a structured system prompt specifying cultural idioms of distress, explanatory models of etiology, factors affecting the therapeutic relationship (stigma, authority dynamics, religious considerations), and cultural strengths. The prompt enforces anti-stereotyping constraints: cultural factors must be woven into the patient narrative rather than isolated as metadata, and within-culture variation is mandated.

#### Design measures intended to reduce demographic stereotyping.

To prevent the generation of harmful stereotypes or essentialist caricatures, three independent safeguards were enforced throughout development:

- • Orthogonal demographic sampling: Cultural identities were sampled independently of the diagnostic distribution, so that in expectation specific conditions (such as substance use disorders, somatic symptom disorders, or severe psychosis) were not disproportionately paired with minoritized groups. Independent sampling constrains the expected pairing but does not guarantee balance in any finite corpus, and residual imbalances were not separately audited.

- • Within-culture heterogeneity: System instructions explicitly mandated varied degrees of acculturation, healthcare literacy, and traditional identification within each demographic group.

- • Multi-round psychiatrist audit: The 54-member board-certified psychiatrist panel audited all candidate scenarios for clinical realism, demographic plausibility, and cultural fidelity as part of the 8-criterion validation rubric (Criterion 1 and Criterion 8; Appendix C.1.3). Reviewers were not specifically matched to the cultural backgrounds they were reviewing; evaluation was based on clinical plausibility and adherence to the anti-stereotyping criteria rather than lived cultural expertise. Scenarios exhibiting reductive stereotyping or caricature were rejected (Appendix C.1). We acknowledge that clinician-assessed plausibility is a necessary but insufficient proxy for authentic cultural representation, and that validation by members of the represented communities is needed before clinical deployment.

## Appendix D Safety Taxonomy Development

We define taxonomies of safety-challenging patient behaviors for conversational AI, encompassing both mental health and general ambulatory care settings. These taxonomies were developed through structured elicitations with practicing clinicians and modified Delphi consensus.

### D.1 Clinical Safety Taxonomy for Ambulatory Care

The clinical safety taxonomy classifies real-world patient communicative behaviors that create safety risks when large language models serve as clinicians in ambulatory text-based encounters. It addresses clinically motivated patient behaviors and deliberate system exploitation. It excludes system failures independent of patient behavior (e.g., confabulation, privacy) and risks requiring physical infrastructure. This taxonomy structures adversarial training and evaluation by defining the training scenario space and providing a classification scheme for post-hoc failure coding.

We derived the taxonomy through a structured synthesis of five patient safety frameworks, validated by modified Delphi consensus (Table 1a; Supplementary Table 12). We extracted event types from the WHO ICPS 189, AHRQ Common Formats 1, the IOM medical error classification 82, the DEER diagnostic error taxonomy 150, and the Joint Commission Patient Safety Event Taxonomy 18, with concordance confirmed by existing analyses 147. We supplemented these with the cognitive error literature on anchoring and premature closure 28; 29; 55; patient communication and health disparities literature 85; 125; 44; 9; 91; 12; therapeutic alliance ruptures 204; and the adversarial machine learning literature on manipulation attacks against deployed language models 133; 205; 56.

Applying pre-specified decision rules for these criteria triggered six mergers, four clarity revisions, and the addition of two new items: stigma-driven non-disclosure and goals-of-care misalignment.

## Appendix E Related Work

Medical artificial intelligence has progressed from rule-based systems to deep learning classifiers, foundation models, and interactive agentic systems. Here, we apply multi-turn reinforcement learning to psychiatric intake by training a clinical AI agent within a simulated environment to jointly optimize diagnostic reasoning and patient-centered communication.

#### Foundational medical AI and clinical reasoning.

Early clinical AI systems used handcrafted rule bases and probabilistic inference for diagnostic decision-making, such as MYCIN 158, whereas deep learning later enabled high-accuracy, single-task diagnostic classifiers for specialized modalities 36; 174; 143. Multimodal foundation models subsequently demonstrated broad clinical reasoning 162; 163; 113, achieving strong performance on medical question-answering benchmarks including MedQA-USMLE 74, MedMCQA 126, and MMLU clinical subdomains 66. Advanced prompting and multi-agent collaborative frameworks such as MedAgents 172 enable generalist models to match specialized systems 120, while retrieval-augmentation and external tools extend real-time knowledge access 200; 105 and single-turn RL models improve diagnostic accuracy on verifiable cases 89. Because these advances remain confined to static single-turn settings, early conversational clinical models 97; 60; 181 sought to establish interactive dialogue, though without rigorous multi-turn clinical evaluation.

AMIE 176 represented a milestone, showing that self-play supervised fine-tuning and blinded OSCE-style evaluations produce a system matching primary care physicians on history-taking, communication, and diagnostic accuracy. Subsequent advances expanded this paradigm to complex differential diagnosis 109, multimodal specialist care 124, consumer symptom elicitation 13, and prospective clinical deployment 15. However, these systems focused on general medical consultations rather than optimizing across the sequential decision chains under diagnostic uncertainty and rapport-dependent disclosure that characterize psychiatric encounters.

#### Long-horizon reinforcement learning for clinical decision-making.

Medical decision analysis frames sequential decision-making under uncertainty through Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) 63; 186. Historically, healthcare reinforcement learning focused on retrospective offline RL to optimize low-dimensional treatments from EHR records, including sepsis and hemodynamic control 83; 142; 132 (reviewed in Yu et al. Super; Coronato et al. Super), whereas language model preference alignment originated with single-step reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) 21; 153; 123; 6 and direct preference optimization (DPO) 141.

Zhang et al. Super distinguish single-step alignment from multi-turn agentic reinforcement learning, which optimizes policies over temporally extended POMDP trajectories alongside process-supervised step-level reward modeling 101 and text-based feedback 198. Paired with simulators, this approach yields emergent capabilities in competitive games 160; 179, mathematical reasoning via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) 155, and autonomous LLM agents 193. Clinical consultations naturally fit this formulation because the patient’s psychiatric state remains latent, information emerges sequentially through targeted inquiry, and optimal management depends on prior conversational decisions.

Concurrent systems have begun applying dialogue RL to clinical interaction beyond $T{=}1$ : Doctor-R1 88 uses experience replay to ground updates in successful trajectories, DoctorAgent-RL 41 validates proactive questioning with patients, DiagAgent 140 trains agents within an EHR-grounded world model, SALUS 48 applies per-step GRPO with multi-agent role decomposition, and Multi-Agent CFlow 184 mitigates premature diagnostic closure using hierarchical action spaces. However, these systems focus on general medical dialogue loops or structured diagnostic ordering rather than psychiatric presentations and rapport-gated communication. Our simulation framework jointly optimizes multi-turn inquiry, clinical documentation, management planning, and patient-centered communication within a long-horizon RL environment.

#### AI in psychiatric care and clinical communication.

Mental healthcare AI spans early conversational systems, rule-based interventions, language biomarkers, and foundation model agents. Early work highlighted safety vulnerabilities when conversational agents encountered crises 112, while structured digital interventions demonstrated clinical impact: Woebot reduced depressive symptoms in a randomized trial 43, and Limbic Access increased referral completion by 15% among 129,400 UK NHS patients 59. Human-AI collaboration has also shown benefit, with AI suggestions improving counselor empathy by 19.6% on crisis hotlines 156 and public evaluations rating LLM responses higher in quality and empathy than physician responses 5. Scoping and systematic reviews map generative AI applications across behavioral healthcare 70; 116; 57, position papers outline responsible deployment frameworks 166; 175; 31, and recent meta-analyses quantify the clinical evidence base for LLM chatbots 202; 34.

Fine-tuned foundation-model agents represent a further shift: Therabot reduced depression and anxiety in a randomized trial 65, and a three-arm RCT found a conversational AI agent non-inferior to face-to-face group therapy for depression and superior for anxiety reduction 159. Specialized models include MentaLLaMA 195 for social media depression detection, SoulChat 19 and MindChat 157 for emotional support, AutoCBT 194 for autonomous Cognitive Behavioral Therapy, PsycoLLM 69 for psychological evaluation, and PsychAgent 196 for evolving therapeutic skills via rejection fine-tuning. In clinician-facing settings, PsychFound 183 and Kim and Rodriguez Super demonstrated decision-support utility, while multi-agent architectures have been applied to structured clinical interviewing 79, psychotherapy fidelity assessment 78, and psychiatry residency training 146.

In parallel, computational language and speech processing has yielded objective digital biomarkers predicting psychosis onset 23. Existing mental health AI systems largely operate as single-turn classifiers, open-ended support chatbots, or offline prediction tools, rather than training a clinical agent via reinforcement learning to execute complete psychiatric intake encounters that integrate diagnostic investigation with structured, patient-centered communication.

#### Clinical simulation environments.

Simulation fidelity sets the upper bound for agent competence training in medical education 7; 22. Building on generative multi-agent simulations 129 and early clinical dialogue ontologies 38, recent platforms introduce multi-agent virtual hospitals 95, persona-driven profiles 86, temperament-conditioned consultations 171, state-aware simulators 98, generative patient state evolution 115, and dynamic clinical environment evaluation 106. Agentic evaluation suites also assess tool use in provider-facing EHR workflows (MedAgentBench 73, FHIR-AgentBench 93), clinical data modeling (HealthAgentBench 103), and patient-facing primary care workflows across multi-turn exchanges (PatientAgentBench 178).

Existing patient simulators predominantly function as cooperative environments where simulated patients willingly disclose clinical information upon request. In actual psychiatric practice, patients frequently withhold history, minimize symptoms, and resist treatment recommendations 10; 39; 25. Our simulation environment addresses this gap with a stratified information disclosure architecture in which critical clinical facts remain gated behind specific behavioral triggers, including direct targeted inquiry, empathic rapport, and sustained trust.

#### Evaluating AI in psychiatry.

PsychBench 104 established an evaluation framework for LLMs in psychiatric practice across 16 models with a 60-psychiatrist reader study, while PsychiatryBench 46 extends evaluation across multiple tasks, MindBench.ai 35 engages clinicians, researchers, and individuals with lived experience, and PsychEval 128 introduces a multi-session evaluation spanning 369 cases across five therapeutic modalities. MindEval 138 tests models on extended 20–40 turn mental health dialogues, MENTAT 90 provides a clinician-annotated dataset of real-world tasks and ambiguity, MedDialogRubrics 54 develops fine-grained clinician rubrics for multi-turn consultations, and ALFA 96 aligns models for targeted questioning during diagnostic reasoning, complementing interactive general-medical benchmarks such as CRAFT-MD 77 and AgentClinic 152 as well as static single-turn benchmarks such as MedQA 74, MedMCQA 126, and PubMedQA 76.

Whereas existing frameworks primarily assess static medical knowledge, single-dimension conversational fluency, or isolated diagnostic accuracy 8; 75, psychiatric intake requires establishing trust to elicit gated information, reasoning under diagnostic ambiguity, and formulating management plans aligned with the patient’s relational context. Our simulated intake evaluation provides 127 expert-curated scenarios with stratified disclosure requirements to assess whether an agent can elicit information from guarded patients and formulate safe, appropriate care plans.

#### Safety, equity, and red-teaming in clinical AI.

Deploying AI in psychiatry presents distinct safety risks, illustrated by documented adverse events such as a chatbot providing calorie-counting advice to eating disorder patients 187, over-validation of distorted client thoughts 72, stigmatizing responses 114, unsafe medical guidance 33, and omission of crisis resources such as the 988 lifeline during emergencies 178. Frameworks for responsible healthcare machine learning emphasize avoiding clinical harm 188 and verifying factual grounding 192, while equity audits highlight algorithmic disparities in clinical risk prediction 122 and clinical vignettes 199, motivating health-equity evaluation toolboxes 135 and intersectional analyses 27. Adversarial red-teaming methodologies for general LLMs 133 have recently been extended to mental health support 167, where regulatory frameworks such as the EU AI Act classify systems interacting with vulnerable populations as high-risk 164.

Our evaluation framework incorporates adversarial safety testing through a dual-taxonomy design (clinical safety and mental health relational competence) validated via independent modified Delphi consensus, providing a structured methodology for detecting clinical safety vulnerabilities under deceptive, manipulative, and boundary-testing patient presentations.
